Under sub-section (1) of section 83, the competent authority has power of provisional attachment, where during pendency of any proceedings under the Act he is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of government revenue, it is necessary so to do. Such provisional attachment could be of any property including the bank account of the taxable person. Sub-section (2) of section 83, however, provided that every such provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of one year from the date of which such order has been made. [Para 15]

In the instant case, nothing is demonstrated by the department either in the orders of attachment or in the affidavit filed. The reason why exercise of such drastic power of attachment of bank accounts was necessary. Therefore, such attachments are set aside. At the same time, some security is provided so that eventually, if the tax liability is confirmed, the department is not left with no means to recover the same. [Para 16]

Thus, the respondents shall return the petitioner's three cheques collected on 20-2-2018. Second show-cause notice dated 19-03-2018 is set aside leaving it open for the department to consider only on the ground of lack of jurisdiction and not on merits of the demand sought to be raised in this show-cause notice. The provisional attachment of the petitioner's two bank accounts is removed. [Para 17]

1)

The order of provisional attachment before the assessment order is made, may be justified if the Assessing Authority or any other authority empowered in law is of the opinion that it is necessary to protect the interest of revenue. However, the subjective satisfaction should be based on some credible materials or information and also should be supported by supervening factor. It is not any and every material, howsoever vague and indefinite or distant remote or far fetching, which would warrant the formation of the belief.

(2) The power conferred upon the authority under section 83 for provisional attachment could be termed as a very drastic and far reaching power. Such power should be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and reasons.

(3)

The power of provisional attachment under section 83 should be exercised by the authority only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and caution.

(4)

The power under section 83 for provisional attachment should be exercised only if there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of wholly or any part of his/her property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of demand and in order to achieve the said objective, the attachment should be of the properties and to that extent, it is required to achieve this objective.

(5)

The power under section 83 should neither be used as a tool to harass the assessee nor should it be used in a manner which may have an irreversible detrimental effect on the business of the assessee.

(6)

The attachment of bank account and trading assets should be resorted to only as a last resort or measure. The provisional attachment under section 83 should not be equated with the attachment in the course of the recovery proceedings.

(7)

The authority before exercising power under section 83 for provisional attachment should take into consideration two things: (i) whether it is a revenue neutral situation (ii) the statement of 'output liability or input credit'. Having regard to the amount paid by reversing the input tax credit if the interest of the revenue is sufficiently secured, then the authority may not be justified in invoking its power under section 83 for the purpose of provisional attachment. [Para 52]

Thus, the respondents have not acted in accordance with law. [Para 53]

The writ application succeeds and is allowed. The assessment order dated 17-6-2019 passed by the respondent No. 4, Commercial Tax Officer at Vadodara demanding total amount of Rs. 1,60,79,302 towards tax, penalty and interest is hereby quashed and set aside. However, it is clarified that if the authority wants to proceed against the writ applicant under section 74, then it shall be open for the authority to do so after issuing appropriate show cause notice and give an opportunity of hearing to the writ applicant. [Para 54]

The order of provisional attachment of the stock of goods dated 27-11-2018 as well as the order of provisional attachment of the writ applicant's current account is quashed and set aside. The blockage of input tax credit dated 13-2-2019 by way of computer entry is also held to be illegal and is ordered to be released forthwith. [Para 55]

Further, the subjective satisfaction which had been arrived at by an authority could not be requested to be set at naught in extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court in the absence of any mala fide in the petition. Such discretion of an authority could not be usurped by the Court under article 226 of the Constitution of India. HELD: The authority has come to a particular conclusion after satisfying itself on the basis of material which has already been produced by the assessee and found that action is necessitated in the interest of revenue. When the decision is taken on the basis of material and information which were received, the action taken by authorities cannot be said to be either perverse or impermissible in law more particularly when the proceedings are already set into motion. [Para 6]

The proceedings in the form of show-cause notice of tax ascertained being payable by the assessee under section 74 of the Act has already been initiated and a specific notice in form GST DRC-01 is already issued under rule 142(1). It is quite clear that when the statutory function is being undertaken by authorities and when there is no allegation of specific mala fides, the function of the authority, in view of settled position of law, cannot be usurped by the High Court in exercise of extraordinary equitable jurisdiction when a satisfaction is arrived at by an authority that interest of revenue deserves to be protected. Hence, in the absence of any material or patent illegality such satisfaction cannot be disturbed or substituted for the sake of substitution and background of fact is such where the process cannot be intercepted when it has already commenced. [Para 8]

When the substantial justice is pitted against technical consideration, predominance is given to the substantial justice. Hence, when the authority is out to take a step in the interest of revenue and show cause notice is already issued, the petition challenging the order of attachment was not entertained. [Para 9]

It has been clearly asserted by authority that amendment of section 83 of the CGST Act covers various chapters. The said chapters include the proceedings under section 70 of the Act. As such if the proceedings are carried out by an authority is pending, the authorities have power to initiate proceedings under section 83 of the CGST Act. [Para 14]

In the absence of any specific mala fides of any nature and since the process is initiated by an authority in any manner the equitable extraordinary jurisdiction cannot be exercised as the authority has arrived at a subjective satisfaction on the basis of material on record. [Para 15]

any manner empowered or entitled to initiate an action against its customers without there being any cogent material on record that has been provided to the bank from formal entities such as the Reserve Bank of India, Central Bureau of Investigating, Enforcement Directorate, police authorities amongst others. In every such instance where a designated authority approaches the bank to take action against any of the accounts of the customers of the bank, the designated authority is also required to provide some proof of certain suspicious activities. [Para 29]

■ As is evident from the above judgment, any action that is taken by any authority has to be backed up with relevant information and must be on the basis of a complaint lodged either before the police or by approaching the magistrate. In any event, none of the provisions under the various legislations governing bank accounts allow freezing of a bank account by the bank authority on its own volition without there being an underlying complaint. The only instance when the bank can freeze an account in its own volition is when the bank has a lien on the said account by virtue of certain loans having been taken by the customer (see: Section 171 of the Contract Act,1872). In the absence of such a lien no authority is present with a bank to stop the operation of an account of a customer and any such action without the authority of law is a degenerative, arbitrary, perverse and mala fide action that is an anathema to the rule of law and is required to be struck down heavily at the very first instance it comes before the courts of law. [Para 31]

■

Accordingly, the present writ petition is Allowed in the aforesaid terms. [Para 32]

■

Before parting, this Court is constrained to observe that there is an increasing menace these days of freezing bank account indiscriminately. Admittedly, in the present case the Respondent-Bank has frozen the bank account of the petitioner, without any rhyme or reason and the same is not permissible as per law. Since, such indiscriminate freezing has the inevitable effect of paralysing the day-to-day business operations of the petitioner, resulting in loss of commercial goodwill and financial consequences, a cost of Rs. 50,000/- (Fifty thousand Only) is hereby imposed on the Respondent-Indian Overseas Bank, Alambagh branch, Lucknow, through the Branch Manager as a compensation to the petitioner. The said cost shall be payable to the petitioner within a period of four weeks from the date a certified copy of this judgment is served on the Respondent-Bank. [Para 33]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority for recovery of dues of Rs. 14.62 crores had provisionally attached various bank accounts of assessee - Whether since assessee had already reversed input tax credit to tune of Rs. 13.28 crores, interest of revenue was sufficiently secured - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, provisional attachment of bank accounts of assessee was no longer justified - Held, yes - Whether Competent Authority was to be directed to forthwith release provisional attachment over bank accounts of assessee - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of assessee]GST: Where Competent Authority for recovery of dues of Rs. 14.62 crores had provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee, since assessee had already reversed input tax credit to tune of Rs. 13.28 crores, interest of revenue was sufficiently secured and, therefore, provisional attachment of bank accounts was no longer justified

FACT: The Competent Authority for recovery of GST dues had provisionally attached various bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking directions to the Competent Authority to release all bank accounts.

HELD: The impugned order of provisional attachment has been made in exercise of powers under section 83. Section 83 inter alia provides that where during the pendency of any proceedings under section 67 or section 73 or section 74, the Commissioner is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue, it is necessary so to do, he may, by an order in writing attach provisionally any property, including bank account, belonging to the taxable person in such manner as may be prescribed. [Para 9]

At the time when the impugned order under section 83 came to be passed, according to the Competent Authority, an amount of Rs. 14.62 crores would have been due and payable by the assessee. [Para 10]

Under section 83, the Commissioner is empowered to order provisional attachment for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. In the facts of the instant case, while a liability of Rs. 14.62 crores had been estimated at the time when the order under section 83 came to be passed, the present estimate is Rs. 16.24 crores. Thus the assessee upon conclusion of any proceedings that may be taken pursuant to the proceedings under section 67 or section 73 or section 74 may be liable to pay such amount. Admittedly the assessee has already reversed input tax credit to the tune of Rs. 13.28 crores. Considering the amount paid by reversing input tax credit, the interest of the revenue is sufficiently secured. Therefore, the provisional attachment of the bank accounts of the assessee is no longer justified. [Para 11]

In view of the aforesaid, the Competent Authority was to be directed to forthwith release the provisional attachment over the bank accounts of the assessee. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, read with section 8 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992/Section 83 of the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Whether property including bank account liable to or which has been provisionally attached must belong to taxable person - Held, yes - Whether suspension and cancellation of importer exporter code number can be done only under Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 by Director General of Foreign Trade or by his authorized officer for reasons specified and in manner provided in section 8 of Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 - Held, yes - Petitioner, sole proprietor, was engaged in business of export of various products - For goods exported out of India, petitioner claimed various export incentives - Department carried out search operations in residence and office premises of petitioner whereafter various documents etc. were seized - Consequently, importer exporter code of petitioner was blocked and accounts belonging to him and his family members freezed - From list of bank accounts, it was seen that 3 bank accounts were in joint names of petitioner, and his wife and one account was solely in name of his wife - There was no allegation made by department that any money belonging to petitioner or to his firm had been credited into joint accounts of petitioner with his wife or with his minor son or into account of his wife - Whether, on facts, joint account and account belonging to his wife would be unfrozen - Held yes - Whether blocking of Importer Exporter Code of petitioner by any authority other than Director General of Foreign Trade or by his authorized officer under section 8 would be unauthorized, unwarranted and without jurisdicition - Held, yes [Paras 22-25]GST : Where after search, accounts belonging to petitioner and his family members had been freezed, since there was no allegation made by department that money belonging to petitioner or to his firm had been credited into joint accounts of petitioner with his wife or with his minor son or into account of his wife, joint accounts of petitioner with his wife would be unfrozen

FACT: The petitioner was the sole proprietor of a proprietorship firm and was engaged in the business of export of various products.

For the goods exported out of India, the petitioner claims various export incentives.

With regard to export incentives claimed by the petitioner, department carried out search operations in the residence and office premises of the petitioner on 11-9-2019 whereafter various documents, etc., were seized. Simultaneously, the importer exporter code of the petitioner was blocked and accounts belonging to him and his family members freezed.

On writ:

HELD: From a careful analysis of section 83 read with sub-rule (1) of rule 159 what is to be noted is that the property including the bank account liable to or which has been provisionally attached must belong to the taxable person. 'Taxable person' has been defined in section 2(107) of the CGST Act to mean a person who is registered or is liable to be registered under section 22 or 24. [Para 19]

The department have explained in their affidavits that the investigation carried out against the petitioner fell within the ambit of sections 67 and 74 and provisional attachment orders were issued in the prescribed format. [Para 20]

Contention of the petitioner that there was violation of the provisions of section 83 and no due process was followed while provisionally attaching the bank accounts and the rebuttal contentions of the respondents that there has been due compliance to the statutory requirement of section 83 read with rule 159 may require a detailed examination. As regards the attachment of the bank accounts from the perspective of the taxable person, from the list of bank accounts, it is seen that the three bank accounts are in the joint names of petitioner's wife and petitioner whereas one bank account is solely in the name of petitioner's wife. It has been clarified that 'M' and 'M' Mandavia is one and the same person and is the wife of the petitioner. On the other hand it was found that other bank accounts are in the joint names of the petitioner and his (minor) son. Prima facie, 'M' and minor son are not the concerned taxpayers in this case. There are no allegations against them. To be more specific, there was no allegation made by the department that any money belonging to the petitioner or to his firm had been credited into the joint accounts of the petitioner with his wife or with his minor son or into the account of his wife. As a matter of fact, department have stated that the reason for attachment of other bank accounts appears to be their link with the petitioner or his PAN. They being not the taxpayers in this case, provisional attachment of their bank accounts, therefore, would not be justified. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 132 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Search and seizure - General (Freezing of bank accounts) - Whether as per section 132(8-A), order of freezing bank accounts could not remain in force for a period exceeding sixty days from date of order - Held, yes - During search and seizure operation under section 132, several persons/entities were found to be involved in hawala transactions through bogus RTGS and crypto currencies - Pursuant to same and on basis of certain suspicious transactions, accounts of assessees were debit frozen to avoid leakage of revenue - Whether since, order in question was issued on 30-4-2023, rigour period stood concluded by 30-6-2023, therefore, perpetuation of freezing of bank accounts beyond 60 days was completely unsustainable and de hors provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, letter dated 30-4-2023 having already lived out its life and ceased to have any significance by virtue of operation of law, same was to be declared unenforceable and there was to be a direction to immediately de-freeze concerned bank accounts of assessees - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 12] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where pursuant to search and seizure operation conducted in case of certain persons, bank accounts of assessees were debit frozen to avoid leakage of revenue, perpetuation of freezing of bank accounts beyond 60 days was completely unsustainable and de hors provisions, hence, there was to be a direction to immediately de-freeze concerned bank accounts of assessees

Section 132 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Search and seizure - General (Freezing of bank accounts) - Whether as per section 132(8-A), order of freezing bank accounts could not remain in force for a period exceeding sixty days from date of order - Held, yes - During search and seizure operation under section 132, several persons/entities were found to be involved in hawala transactions through bogus RTGS and crypto currencies - Pursuant to same and on basis of certain suspicious transactions, accounts of assessees were debit frozen to avoid leakage of revenue - Whether since, order in question was issued on 30-4-2023, rigour period stood concluded by 30-6-2023, therefore, perpetuation of freezing of bank accounts beyond 60 days was completely unsustainable and de hors provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, letter dated 30-4-2023 having already lived out its life and ceased to have any significance by virtue of operation of law, same was to be declared unenforceable and there was to be a direction to immediately de-freeze concerned bank accounts of assessees - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: A search and seizure operation dated 28-4-2023 was conducted under section 132(1) and it was found that several persons/entities were involved in hawala transactions through bogus RTGS and cryptocurrencies. Pursuant to the said search and seizure operation and on the basis of certain suspicious transactions, the accounts of the assessees were debit frozen to avoid leakage of revenue.

The assessees by way of instant petition, sought directions to de-freeze the bank accounts and to set aside the letter dated 30-4-2023 issued by the respondents.

The assessee submitted that as per the mandate of section 132(8-A), the freezing of bank accounts ceases to have effect after the expiry of a period of sixty days. He, therefore, submitted that since the maximum period for which the bank accounts could have been frozen had already expired on 30-6-2023, there was no reason to proscribe the assessees to operate the bank accounts under consideration.

HELD: Undisputedly, a plain reading of sub-section (8-A) to section 132 would unambiguously signify that in the instant case, the order of freezing the bank accounts could not remain in force for a period exceeding sixty days from the date of the order. Admittedly, the said period of sixty days had already expired before the filing of the present petitions and no subsequent order appears to have been passed for extending the freezing of accounts. Since the order in question was issued on 30-4-2023, the rigour period stood concluded by 30-6-2023, therefore, the perpetuation of freezing of the bank accounts is completely unsustainable and de hors the provisions of the Act. [Para 9]

It is thus seen that despite being extended reasonable indulgence to explain the tenability of the impugned action, the revenue has failed to tender any justification, much less a cogent explanation which could sustain such action. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section  12,  read with section  12AA,  of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and  section 171    of the Contract Act, 1872 and section  102  of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 - Reporting entity to maintain records - Petitioner, a sole proprietor engaged in sale and purchase of fisheries machineries, maintained a current account with respondent bank - During business, Rs. 23 lakhs was received by RTGS from one Mrs. Anita allegedly towards purchase of machineries, and Rs. 5 lakhs was withdrawn same day - On attempting further withdrawal thereafter, petitioner was orally informed that account had been frozen; no written order, notice or reasons were communicated - Bank stated that it froze account as a 'suspicious transaction' because petitioner had declared annual income of Rs. 5.76 lakhs at account opening, yet Rs. 23 lakhs was credited and Rs. 5 lakhs withdrawn same day - It relied on Section 12(2) of PMLA to justify freeze as a precaution to restrict further debits - Whether Section 12 of PMLA does not in any manner authorise or remotely concerns freezing of a bank account by banking company itself - Held, yes - Whether since there was neither any complaint by Bank of Maharashtra nor any order from any Competent Authority nor any proceedings had been initiated by said Bank against said Smt. FACT: ■

The petitioner, a sole proprietor of a GST-registered firm engaged in sale and purchase of fisheries machineries, maintained a current account with the respondent bank. About Rs. 23 lakhs was credited to this account via RTGS from one Mrs. Anita allegedly towards purchase of machinery, and about Rs. 5 lakhs was withdrawn the same day. Shortly thereafter, when the petitioner attempted further withdrawal, bank officials orally informed that the account had been frozen. Despite repeated approaches, a text message to the Branch Manager, and a complaint/legal notice, the freeze continued, leading to this writ petition.

■

The respondent bank stated that it froze the account due to suspicious transactions, citing that the petitioner had declared annual income of about Rs. 5.76 lakhs at the time of opening the current account while a large sum of about Rs. 23 lakhs was credited and Rs. 5 lakhs was withdrawn the same day. It relied on Section 12(2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 to justify the freeze as a precaution to restrict further debits, issued a letter seeking transaction details, and on its inquiry stated that the Rs. 23 lakhs was credited by Bank of Maharashtra under a loan to Smt. Anita and that Bank of Maharashtra requested by email that the amount not be released and be refunded.

■

Before the High Court on writ petition.

■

The freezing orders dated 5-9-2018, being cryptic in nature and founded solely on mere suspicion, do not meet the standard prescribed, which is the formation of a "reason to believe". "Suspicion" cannot be equated to a "reason to believe". In fact, suspicion cannot also be equated with a "prima facie" opinion. [Para 59]

■ Although section 17(1A) does not expressly use the phrase "reason to believe", it cannot be read in isolation from section 17(1). The operation of section 17(1A) is intrinsically linked to the practicability of effecting a seizure under section 17(1), and such seizure can only be undertaken upon the formation of a "reason to believe". Since the act of freezing is merely an alternative to seizure, it cannot logically be subjected to a lower or different standard of satisfaction than that applicable to the act of seizure itself. [Para 62]

■

The freezing orders dated 5-9-2018 issued by the ED also fail to disclose the specific material or basis on which such action was necessitated. They merely make a general reference to the amounts in the accounts being involved in money laundering. Such freezing orders do not satisfy the statutory requirements envisaged under sub-sections (1) and (1A) of section 17 of the PMLA. [Para 63]

■

Further, it is opined that, in the present cases, the Appellant has attempted to improve upon its case by subsequently furnishing reasons in its application under Section 17(4), as well as through pleadings, oral submissions, and written arguments. This approach runs contrary to the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in OPTO Circuit India Ltd. v. Axis Bank [2021] 127 taxmann.com 290/165 SCL 703 (SC). The Apex Court, relying on the celebrated judgment in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner [1978] 1 SCC 405, categorically held that the legality of an administrative or quasi-judicial action must be tested solely on the basis of the reasoning and material contained in the impugned order or communication itself. Such an order cannot later be justified or sustained by introducing additional grounds through affidavits, pleadings, or oral submissions before the Court.[Para 64]

■

Applying the same principle, it follows that in the present case, any attempt by the ED to supplement or improve the contents of the impugned freezing orders through their submissions cannot cure the fundamental legal infirmities inherent in the Order.[Para 65]

■

It is a settled proposition that the scheme of the PMLA is designed to strike a delicate balance between the extensive powers conferred upon enforcement authorities and the fundamental rights of individuals. For this reason, the statutory provisions governing search and seizure or freezing of property are hedged with procedural safeguards. These safeguards serve as a check against arbitrary action and ensure that any intrusion into private rights is proportionate, lawful, and subject to independent judicial scrutiny. The efficacy of the statutory scheme and the legitimacy of State action under it depends upon scrupulous adherence to these procedural requirements.[Para 66]

■

Equally well-established is the rule of statutory interpretation that when a statute prescribes that a particular act is to be performed in a specified manner, it must be performed in that manner alone or not at all. Deviation from the prescribed procedure is impermissible in law. The record of the present cases unmistakably discloses noncompliance with the mandatory provisions of Sub-sections (1) and (1A) of Section 17 of the PMLA, as well as Rules 3 and 4 of the PMLA (Search and Seizure or Freezing of Property) Rules, 2005. Such non-compliance renders the freezing orders dated 05.09.2018 issued by the ED not only procedurally defective but also substantively contrary to law.[Para 67]

■

It must also be borne in mind that the freezing of a bank account in violation of statutory requirements has far-reaching consequences. Such action directly impinges upon the constitutional right to property guaranteed under Article 300A of the Constitution of India, which mandates that no person shall be deprived of property except in accordance with the authority of law. Any violation of this constitutional safeguard strikes at the very root of the legitimacy of the impugned action and cannot be countenanced.[Para 68]

■

The ED advanced arguments in respect of the contention that even assuming the first limb of Section 8(3)(a) of the PMLA were not applicable, the second limb thereof would certainly have to be taken into account and since proceedings were pending in Court, the freezing order should be sustained. This contention cannot be accepted.[Para 69]

The second significant aspect of sub-rule (5) is the mandatory requirement of furnishing an opportunity of being heard to the person whose property is attached. This is in consonance with the principles of natural justice and ensures that a fair procedure is observed. Sub-rule (5) provides for a post provisional attachment right of:

(i)

Submitting an objection to the attachment;

(ii)

An opportunity of being heard. Sub -rule (5) contains clear language to the effect that a person whose property is attached is entitled to two procedural entitlements: first, the right to submit an objection on the ground that the property was not or is not liable to be attached; and second, an opportunity of being heard to the person filing an objection. This is a clear indicator that in addition the filing of an objection, the person whose property is attached is entitled to an opportunity of being heard. It is not open to the Commissioner, as has been stated in the present case, to hold the view that the only safeguard under sub-rule 5 is to submit an objection without an opportunity of a personal hearing. Such a construction would be plainly contrary to sub-rule 5 which contemplates both the submission of an objection to the attachment and an opportunity of being heard. The opportunity of being heard can be availed of as a matter of right by the person whose property is attached. Both the right to submit an objection and to be afforded an opportunity of being heard are valuable safeguards. The consequence of a provisional attachment is serious. It displaces the person whose property is attached from dealing with the property. Where a bank account is attached, it prevents the person from operating the account. A business entity whose bank account is attached is seriously prejudiced by the inability to utilize the proceeds of the account for the purpose of business. The dual procedural safeguards inserted in sub-rule 5 of rule 159 demand strict compliance.

The Commissioner who hears the objections must pass a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the objections. To allow the Commissioner to get by without passing a reasoned order will make his decision subjective and defeat the purpose of subjecting it to judicial scrutiny. The Commissioner must deal with the objections and pass a reasoned order indicating whether, and if not, why the objections are not being accepted. Sub-rule 6 of rule 159 allows for the release of a property which either was or is no longer liable for attachment. The form in which such an order has to be passed, namely form GST DRC-23, states that 'now there is no such proceeding pending against the defaulting person which warrants attachment' of the account or as the case may be, the property. Sub -rules 5 and 6 do not expressly contemplate a situation in which the person whose property is attached can object on the ground that the attachment is in excess of the amount likely to be due for which proceedings have been launched under the Act. Nor does it provide for a specific opportunity to the taxable person to offer any alternative form of security in lieu of the attachment. Such an opportunity must be read into the provision to allow for a fair working in practice. Whether any alternative security that is furnished by the taxable person should be accepted and if so, its sufficiency, is a matter for the Commissioner to determine. Undoubtedly, the taxable person may not have a right to demand that only a particular form of security must be accepted. The Commissioner has to decide whether the form of security offered would secure the interest of the revenue. Where the taxable person sets up the plea that the extent of the attachment is excessive or where the taxable person offers an alternative form of security, these are also matters which ought to be determined by the Commissioner in the exercise of powers under rule 159(5). The scope of objection can also extend to the nature of the property which is being provisionally attached. Now, it is in this backdrop that it needs to be determined whether the petition under article 226 was maintainable and if it was, whether Commissioner exercised the powers under section 83 read with rule 159 in accordance with law. [Para 56]

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 65, of the Tamil Nadu Value Added Tax Act, 2006 - Recovery of tax - Attachment of bank account - Assessment year 2012-13 - Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) inspected assessee's business premises in terms of section 65 and noticed certain defects and discrepancies in its account books - Thereupon he forcibly collected a cheque for an amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs from assessee towards tax due on alleged defects - Thereafter Assessing Authority concerned having found that department's bank had returned above cheque unrealised issued a notice to bank of assessee attaching its bank account for recovery of above amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs - Whether in light of provisions of sections 45 and 65, issue of notice to bank of assessee straightaway attaching bank account was illegal and unsustainable and in violation of principles of natural justice - Held, yes [Para 11][In favour of assessee]CST  VAT : Where Commercial Tax Officer (CTO) inspected assessee's business premises and having noticed defects in its account books forcibly collected a cheque for Rs. 3.75 lakhs from it and thereafter Assessing Authority concerned having found that department's bank had returned above cheque unrealised issued a notice to bank of assessee attaching its bank account for recovery of above amount, issue of notice to bank of assessee straightaway attaching bank account was illegal and unsustainable

FACT: The assessee was a dealer in electrical components. On 2-8-2012 the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) inspected the assessee's business premises in terms of section 65 and noticed various defects and discrepancies in its account books. Thereupon he forcibly collected a cheque for an amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs from the assessee towards tax due on the alleged defects.

The assessee made a representation before the Assessing Authority concerned, wherein all the defects noticed had been explained and he had been requested to withhold the cheque amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs which was forcibly collected by the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) at the time of inspection.

Thereafter the Assessing Authority having found that the department's bank had returned the above cheque unrealised issued a notice to the bank of assessee attaching its bank account for the recovery of the amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs.

On writ:

HELD: A combined reading of the provisions of sections 45 and 65 makes it crystal clear that though the authorities are vested with ample powers to take action for the recovery of the tax due, such action must be preceded by issuance of a notice demanding such tax following a due assessment. The assessment and demand must be done in accordance with law, namely, after giving an opportunity to the assessee to put forth its defence/explanation for the queries raised, more particularly, in a case of surprise inspection/search. In the instant case, a spot inspection had been conducted by the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) on 2-8-2012 and on the same day a cheuqe for a sum of Rs. 3.75 lakhs was collected from the assessee.

After noticing the discrepancies in the books of account, etc., the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) ought to have either issued a notice to the assessee pointing out all the discrepancies or he should have intimated the discrepancies to the Assessing Authority for further course of action. On the alleged discrepancies, either the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) or the Assessing Authority should have heard the assessee and then pass an order demanding whatever be the tax due therefrom. Even after such a demand, if the assessee had not paid the tax due thereon, by all means, the authorities are empowered to take any action.

In the instant case, a notice pointing out the discrepancies had not been issued to the assessee. No opportunity was afforded to the assessee to put forth its defence. No notice of demand of tax due was served on the assessee. Instead of doing all these things, the Assessing Authority has cast a notice in form U (notice for recovery of money) to the bank straightaway attaching the bank account of the assessee, which is per se illegal and unsustainable and in violation of the principles of natural justice. [Para 11]

Therefore, the impugned notice was liable to be quashed. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 44 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003 read with rule 27 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Rules, 2006 - Returns, assessment and tax administration - Recovery - Special mode of - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Assessing Authority passed assessment orders on assessee and raised tax demand upon it - Against orders of assessment, assessee preferred appeals together with stay applications - In meanwhile on 11-9-2015 Assessing Authority issued on assessee a notice of demand calling upon it to pay demand within a period of three days - Further Assessing Authority on same day, i.e., on 11-9-2005, passed an order under section 44 attaching three bank accounts of assessee - Whether conduct of Assessing Authority in attaching bank accounts under section 44 was not warranted, when appeals together with stay applications were pending consideration before First Appellate Authority - Held, yes - Whether First Appellate Authority was to be directed to decide stay applications within a period of fifteen days - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]CST  VAT : Gujarat VAT - Where against orders of assessment, assessee filed appeals together with stay applications and in meanwhile Assessing Authority issued on assessee a notice of demand and on same day he passed an order under section 44 attaching bank accounts of assessee, conduct of Assessing Authority in attaching bank accounts was not warranted, when appeals together with stay applications were pending consideration before First Appellate Authority

FACT: In relation to the assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13, the Assessing Authority passed assessment orders on the assessee and raised tax demand upon it.

Against the orders of assessment, the assessee preferred appeals within the prescribed period of limitation together with stay applications.

In the meanwhile on 11-9-2015 the Assessing Authority issued on the assessee a notice of demand with interest calling upon it to pay demand within three days.

Further the Assessing Authority on the same day, i.e., on 11-9-2015 passed an order under section 44 and attached the three bank accounts of the assessee. He directed each of the banks to send to him pay order/demand draft of the entire demand covered under the demand notice.

On writ:

HELD: In relation to the above demand with interest, the Assessing Authority had issued notice to the assessee on 11-9-2015 calling upon it to pay the amount under the demand notice within a period of three days, failing which he would initiate recovery proceedings. However, without waiting for the period of three days to elapse, the Assessing Authority on the very same day has attached the three bank accounts of the assessee. [Para 11]

In relation to each of the assessment years, the assessee has filed appeals and the stay applications. All of which are pending before the First Appellate Authority for consideration. However, on the one hand, the First Appellate Authority is not taking any decision on the stay applications and, on the other hand, the Assessing Authority is proceeding to make coercive recovery by attaching the bank accounts of the assessee. [Para 12]

It is true that under rule 27, the Assessing Authority is empowered to call upon the assessee to pay the amount assessed within a period of thirty days from the date of service of such notice. However, when the assessee has preferred an appeal together with the stay application within the prescribed period of limitation, the Assessing Authority is required to act in a reasonable manner in connection with the notice issued under rule 27. The Assessing Authority is required to keep in mind the fact that the assessee has preferred appeals before the First Appellate Authority and that the stay applications are pending.

Under the circumstances, it is expected of the Assessing Authority to stay his hands till the stay applications of the assessee are decided. In the absence of any exceptional circumstances, there is no warrant for the Assessing Authority to proceed to initiate coercive recovery in exercise of powers under section 44 by attaching the bank accounts of the assessee. [Para 13]

When the assessee had already preferred an appeal with a stay application, the least that was expected of the Assessing Authority was to wait for the outcome of the stay application before resorting to coercive measures as has been done in the instant case. Besides the order under section 44 also suffers from the vice of non-application of mind. In the order issued to each of the banks, the Assessing Authority has sought to recover the entire demand covered under the notice from each of the banks. In case there were sufficient funds in each of the bank accounts, the Assessing Authority would have succeeded in recovering thrice the amount covered under the demand notice.

HELD: "The Supreme Court has opined that the word "property" connotes everything which is subject of ownership, corporeal or incorporeal, tangible or intangible, visible or invisible, real or personal ; everything that has an exchangeable value or which goes to make up wealth or estate or status. Therefore, in the premise of these well-settled principles, it cannot be said that the overdraft bank account of the petitioner-company cannot be treated as 'property' within the meaning of that term for the purpose of interpreting Section 17-B of the APGST Act. It is pertinent to note that whatever amount, whether it is borrowed money or own money of the petitioner-company, lying at the credit of the company in the bank account is the property of the company and therefore it is liable to be attached under the provisions of Section 17-B of the APGST Act." (Para 10)

"The language used in sub-section (1) of Section 17-B of the Act is quite clear, plain and unambiguous and it does not admit more than one meaning. The power conferred upon the Assessing Authority under Section 17-B could be invoked during the pendency of any proceeding for the assessment or reassessment of any turnover. The first condition to invoke the power under Section 17-B is that the proceedings for assessment or reassessment should be pending on the date of the provisional attachment. In the instant case, admittedly the assessment proceedings were pending on the date of the impugned proceeding by issuance of notice dated 27th February, 2001. The other condition which should be satisfied for invoking Section 17-B is that the Assessing Authority should form opinion, that resort to Section 17-B procedure is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. If these two conditions co-exist, technically there cannot be any objection to invoke the power conferred upon the Assessing Authority under Section 17-B of the Act with prior permission of the Commissioner. Therefore, it cannot be contended that the Assessing Authority acted illegally and without authority of law in invoking power under Section 17-B of the Act because provisional assessment proceedings were pending before him." (Para 11)

Now it is to be considered whether the security furnished before the Judicial First Class Magistrate's Court could be considered as sufficient security for the purposes of the Act. Section 451 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 which corresponds to section 497 of the Bharathiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhitha, provides for interim release of property produced before any criminal Court. The interim order for custody in terms thereof is only regarding custody pending the conclusion of the criminal proceeding. The mere fact that the Judicial First Class Magistrate's Court released the money to the assessee on furnishing security cannot have any significance in relation to the proceeding of the Income Tax Department under section 281B. Furnishing security before the Magistrate's Court is to ensure compliance with production of the property on being ordered. The security so furnished before the Magistrate's Court in relation to the proceedings before the Court cannot be construed as enuring to secure a likely demand on assessment under section 147. Section 226(4) authorises the Department to apply to a Court in whose custody there is money belonging to the assessee, to meet the tax due from the assessee. However, at the stage when the criminal proceedings have not culminated, it cannot be said that the security furnished before the Magistrate's Court for interim release of property is sufficient security. Moreover, section 226(4) would apply only when assessment is completed. And even coming to the final disposal of property under section 452 Cr.P.C, there could arise rival claims of title, priority etc. Thus, the security furnished before the Magistrate's Court does not sufficiently secure the possible demand by the department. Another point raised by the petitioner is with respect to non-service of the fresh order personally upon the petitioner. As regards the issue as to whether an order passed under Section 3 remains valid after the expiry of one year from the date of the order?, it is held that the actions of the respondent authorities in continuing with the provisional attachment beyond the period of one year and without informing the bank that the provisional attachment seizes to operate after a period of one year is an act that is reprehensible and absolutely contrary to law. Such an arbitrary action has clearly resulted in violation of the petitioners' rights for carrying on business under Article 19(1) of the Constitution of India and under Article 300A of the Constitution of India wherein the petitioners have been deprived of their property without authority of law. This amount should be deposited in the current accounts that have provisionally attached. As regards the issue as to whether the authorities can issue fresh order of provisional attachment/multiple orders under Section 83,it is held that section 83 empowers the competent authority to issue an order for provisional attachment of property including bank accounts if it is of the opinion that such step is necessary for protecting the interest of the Revenue. It is palpably clear that Section 83(2) permits continuation of a provisional attachment order for a period of one year from the date of order after which it ceases to remain in effect. However, there is nothing in the section which indicates that upon completion of the prescribed period, a fresh order cannot be issued. To say this would amount to supplying such requirements into the section which would go against the well-established principles of interpretation of statutes. In the view point of the Court, after the expiry of the time period, the appropriate authority may be of the opinion that such an attachment is further required to protect the interest of Revenue, and may therefore, issue a fresh order upon compliance of the formalities in Section 83(1). Aggrieved by it, the petitioner challenged the said order by filing the instant writ petition. HELD: Section 281B empowers the Assessing Officer to make a provisional attachment of any property of the assessee during the pendency of any proceeding for the assessment or reassessment of any income, even though there is no demand outstanding against the assessee, if he is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so to protect the interests of the revenue. The order of provisional attachment will be made only after obtaining the approval of the Chief Commissioner or Commissioner or Director General or Director. This provision has been made in order to protect the interests of the revenue in cases where the raising of demand is likely to take time because of investigations and there is apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand. In other words, this section gives a power to be exercised during the pendency of any proceedings for assessment or reassessment, so that the assessee did not fritter away or secrete his resources out of the reach of the department when the assessment or reassessment is completed. The expression ‘for the purpose of protecting the interests of the revenue’ occurring in section 281B of the Act is very wide in its meaning. For that reason as a safeguard, prior approval of a higher authority like Chief Commissioner, Commissioner, Director General or Director, has been made a necessary condition. Further, the orders of provisional attachment must be in writing. However, there must be some material on record to show that the Assessing Officer has formed an opinion on the basis whereof it is necessary to attach the property in order to protect the interests of the revenue. The provisional attachment provided under section 281B is more like an attachment before judgment under the Code of Civil Procedure. It is a liability on the property. The Delhi High Court in Dar International v. Asstt. Director of Income- tax [1993] 114 CTR (Delhi) 172 has opined that the provision relating to making an attachment before judgment, i.e., before assessment order is made, is not illegal if the assessing authority is of the opinion that it is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue and the same is supported by supervening factors. However, the power conferred upon the Assessing Officer under section 281B is very drastic far-reaching power and that power has to be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and reasons. To ensure that this power is not misused, a number of safeguards have been provided in the section itself. One thing is clear that this power should be exercised by the Assessing Officer only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and caution. It should not be exercised unless there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of the demand. Moreover, attachment should be made of the properties and to the extent it is required to achieve the above object. It should neither be used as a tool to harass the assessee nor should it be used in a manner which may have an irreversible detrimental effect on the business of the assessee. The Bombay High Court in Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 has opined that attachment should be made, as far as possible, of immovable properties if that can protect the revenue. Attachment of bank accounts and trading assets should be resorted to only as a last resort. In any event, attachment under section 281B should not be equated with attachment in the course of recovery proceedings.

In the premise of the above noted principles and having regard to the facts of this case, the question that arose for consideration was whether the second respondent had exercised the power conferred upon him under section 281B irrationally and without any justification. The facts stated in the counter affidavit of the second respondent and the correctness of which was not denied by the petitioner-assessee spoke for themselves and justified the drastic action taken by the second respondent by passing impugned orders under section 281B to protect the interest of the revenue. It was relevant to note that, according to the second respondent, the petitioner-assessee had so far received about Rs. 50.70 lakhs as donations of which only Rs. 20 lakhs was under attachment. Further, as could be seen from the impugned orders, it was open for the petitioner to operate its bank account except to the extent of balance as of that date and in that regard a communication dated 29-5-2001 was also sent to the concerned bank by the second respondent. Therefore, the assumption of the petitioner-assessee that the impugned order militated against its functioning and its charitable activities was not well founded.

HELD: At the prima facie stage, the revenue contends strongly that the assessee has indulged into revenue defalcation. Possible tax and penalty liabilities are substantial. For this limited purpose of enabling the assessee to create stock and give bank guarantee, it would be open for the assessee to receive payments from its dealers. Upon fulfiling such conditions, the attachment order would automatically stand suspended along with the directions to the assessee's dealers, for not making payment to the assessee, which will also be suspended. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Period July, 2017 to May, 2019 - Competent Authority had provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee under section 83 on allegation that it without physical receipt of goods availed credit on basis of invoices issued by input supplier and thereafter paid GST on basis of output invoices without physical supply of goods to buyers - During relevant period, total input tax availed by assessee aggregated to Rs. 59.49 crores; whereas total tax paid during this period aggregated to Rs. 63.62 crores - Whether since an amount of Rs. 4.13 crores (Rs. 63.62 crores minus Rs. 59.40 crores) had been paid in excess than amount of credit availed, it could not be said that interest of Government revenue was at a stake - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, order of provisional attachment of bank account of assessee required to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 23 and 30][In favour of assessee]GST: Where Competent Authority had provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee on allegation that it without physical receipt of goods availed credit on basis of invoices issued by input supplier and thereafter paid GST on basis of output invoices without physical supply of goods to buyers, since total input tax availed by assessee aggregated to Rs. 59.49 crores; whereas total tax paid aggregated to Rs. 63.62 crores and that as excess amount of Rs. 4.13 crores had been paid by assessee than amount of credit availed, it could not be said that interest of Government revenue was at a stake and, therefore, impugned order deserved to be quashed

FACT: The Competent Authority had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee under section 83 on the allegation that it without physical receipt of goods availed credit on basis of the invoices issued by the input supplier and thereafter paid GST on the basis of the output invoices without physical supply of the goods to the buyers.

Against the impugned order passed by the Competent Authority, the assessee filed a writ application.

It submitted that the allegation levied against it was to the effect that although the goods were not supplied, yet the tax was paid for the purpose of passing the credit. This was suggestive of the fact that, indisputably, no GST was payable, yet the same was paid. Section 9, which is the charging section, contemplates that the GST is payable only when the goods are supplied. The statement of output liability and input credit pertinent to it would indicate that for the period between July, 2017 and May, 2019, the total input credit availed of by it aggregated to Rs. 59.49 crores; whereas the total tax paid during the said period aggregated to Rs. 63.62 crores. The same was indicative of the fact that against the availment of credit of Rs. 59.49 crores, the tax amount to the tune of Rs. 63.62 crores came to be paid. Thus Rs. 4.13 crores had been paid in excess than the amount of credit availed of. If that be so, then there was no question of arriving at the satifaction by the Competent Authority that the interest of the government revenue was protected.

It further submitted that assuming for the moment that the allegation was true and correct and the credits were wrongly availed of, still the tax had been paid though it was not liable to be paid in light of the fact that there was no supply of goods. The availment of credits could be justified on two counts: (1) it was a revenue neutral satisfaction, and (2) the payment of tax although not payable yet was to be treated as if unavailable credits were reversed after they were wrongly availed.

HELD: The only question that falls for consideration is whether the Competent Authority was justified in invoking section 83 for the purpose of passing an order of attachment of the bank accounts. [Para 22]

individual and had no business connection or nexus with his brother; that the books of account were kept as per the provisions of law; that the search and seizure had been initiated merely on the basis of suspicion and hunch and there was no ‘reason to believe’; that fishing and roving enquiry in the name of search was made only to gather information that there was evasion of tax which was unsustainable in the eyes of law; and that no satisfaction was arrived at before the initiation of search and seizure. HELD: The condition precedent for search and seizure is ‘reason to believe’ under section 132 which cannot be equated with ‘reason to suspect’. The expression ‘reason to believe’ postulates belief and the existence of reasons for that belief. The belief must be held in good faith. It cannot be merely a pretence. The expression ‘reason to believe’ does not mean purely subjective satisfaction on part of authority in making the seizure but the reasons for the belief must have a rational connection or a relevant bearing for the formation of the belief, not extraneous or irrelevant for the said purpose. When places of persons of diverse activities and unconnected with each other are searched and their bank accounts are freezed, to get or gather materials and information to form a belief that the assessee is avoiding tax, it is wholly outside the scope of the search and seizure under the Act. The bank accounts of persons unconnected with the petitioner and reflected in their return were kept under the prohibitory order even after 60 days, which was bad, illegal and should be set aside. That attitude of the respondent-authorities, in making fishing and roving enquiries reflected that the authorities were not in a position to form their opinion for search and seizure. On the other hand, by such activities, the authorities had interfered with the right of the petitioner protected under article 19(1)(g) read with article 300A of the Constitution of India. [Para 8]

Because one was running business of selling products of ‘Haldiram Bhujiawala’ in the name of ‘PFP’, it could not be said that he was liable for block assessment. Flourishing business under the brand name cannot be the reason to believe evasion of tax. Even requirement of block assessment ipso facto cannot be the ‘reason to believe’ under section 132. Section 132 has its independent face value. If one is attracted by such section, he can be assessed in a proper manner under the prescription of law. If one is not so attracted, then there is no question of any block assessment on the basis of search and seizure. Prescription of law about ‘reason to believe’ in the Income-tax Act and the Central Excise Act or the Customs Act is different. In the cases of the Central Excise Act or the Customs Act, ‘reason to believe’ is the sole requirement. But under the Income-tax Act, ‘reason to suspect’ is also available but subject to ‘reason to believe’. Therefore, ‘reason to suspect’ in sub-sections (1A) and (4A) is subject to satisfaction of the primary test of ‘reason to believe’ under section 132(1). In other words, unless one successfully crosses the hurdel of ‘reason to believe’ under section 132(1), there is no scope to get attracted by sub-sections (1A) and (4A). Therefore, the ‘reason to believe’ is the mandatory requirement of law for search and seizure. [Para 30]

FACT: The assessee received a summons under section 70 of the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 from the authorities, directing the assessee to submit copy of GST payment along with other necessary details. The assessee appeared before the authority and submitted all necessary documents in response to the said summons. Thereafter another summons was issued which was replied by assessee. On the basis of reply furnished by assessee, the authority instructed the assessee to submit further documents, specific reasons and details as to why the input tax credit was wrongly claimed.

Subsequently, the proceedings were also initiated and a tax liability of certain amount was presumed by the authority since the assessee had claimed wrongful input tax credit and as such, with a view to safeguard the interest of revenue, by resorting to section 83 of the Act, the bank accounts were sought to be provisionally attached.

Instant writ petition was filed challenging the order of provisional attachment on the ground of violation of principles of natural justice. It was submitted by the assessee that to recover any amount of tax, interest and penalty, firstly, the assessment should be framed, and secondly, the demand notice should be issued and no conditions were fulfilled before attaching the bank account under section 83 of the CGST Act.

On the other hand, it was submitted by the department that the proceedings were already initiated under section 74 of Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 and to protect the interest of revenue, the bank account of assessee were attached by passing an order under section 83 of the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017. Further, the subjective satisfaction which had been arrived at by an authority could not be requested to be set at naught in extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court in the absence of any mala fide in the petition. Such discretion of an authority could not be usurped by the Court under article 226 of the Constitution of India.

DRC-13 on 9-6-2022, challan dated 5-7-2022 and the actual remittance by respondent no. 2 on 12-7-2022 took place squarely during the subsistence of the moratorium. Section 14 imposes a prohibition on the institution or continuation of any recovery proceedings or enforcement action, including attachment, garnishee directions, or debit operations upon the corporate debtor’s bank accounts. [Para 6.3]

■ In the instant case, the applicant has also expressly and repeatedly informed the respondents regarding the initiation of CIRP and the moratorium imposed under section 14, categorically clarifying that any hold, appropriation or freeze placed by statutory authorities such as the GST or State Tax Department cannot survive once moratorium is in force. [Para 6.4]

■

The respondents have sought to justify their actions by contending that respondent no. 2 had no knowledge of the CIRP at the time of remittance and that respondent no. 1 acted under statutory mandate. However, the material on record clearly demonstrates that the erstwhile IRP, by letter dated 8-10-2020, had specifically informed respondent no. 2 of his appointment and directed it not to permit any withdrawals without his authorization. Further, respondent no. 1 was itself informed of the CIRP and the prevailing moratorium by communication dated 27-7-2022. These communications render the defence of lack of knowledge untenable. Even otherwise, the statutory bar under section 14 is automatic and absolute and operates irrespective of the subjective knowledge of the parties. The Supreme Court in Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. [2021] 126 taxmann.com 132/166 SCL 237 (SC), has affirmed that no authority, State or otherwise, may enforce recovery during moratorium and that Section 238 gives overriding effect to the Code over all other laws.[Para 6.5]

■

As regards the appropriation of ₹ 83.89 lakhs, such action directly defeats the scheme of the Code. Government dues occupy a lower priority under section 53 and cannot be recovered in preference to other stakeholders. By withdrawing the amount during moratorium, respondents no. 1 and 2 have effectively accorded themselves priority outside the statutory waterfall mechanism. [Para 6.6]

■

With respect to the freezing of bank accounts, it is noted that the GST authorities have continued appropriation even after commencement of CIRP. Such action directly impedes the RP’s statutory mandate under section 25 to take control and custody of the assets and manage the operations of the corporate debtor as a going concern. Therefore, the continued freeze of the corporate debtor’s accounts with HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank cannot be sustained. [Para 6.7]

■

The contention of respondent no. 1 that its claim stands diminished or extinguished merely because it has recovered ₹ 83.89 lakhs is also misplaced. The recovery, having been undertaken in violation of section 14, is void in law. While the legality of the action forms part of the instant IA, the validity of the underlying statutory dues is not affected by such irregular recovery. Any legitimate claim of respondent no. 1 must be adjudicated and collated in accordance with the Code and CIRP Regulations and cannot be enforced through unilateral recovery. [Para 6.8]

■

In view of the foregoing discussion, it is held and directed that: (a) the recovery of ₹ 83.89 lakhs by respondents no. 1 and 2 during moratorium is in violation of section 14 and hence void; (b) the said amount is liable to be refunded to the corporate debtor through the applicant/RP and (c) attachments/freezing of all bank accounts of the corporate debtor maintained with respondents no. 2, 3 and 4 must be lifted forthwith to enable conduct of CIRP in accordance with law. [Para 6.9]

headnotes.text: GST : Where on spot visit, flying squad opined that purchases made by writ-applicant from two parties were not genuine and hence, collected documents and books of account and passed order of provisional attachment of two bank accounts, having regard to fact that there was hardly a balance of Rs.22,065 in two bank accounts, there was no good reason to continue provisional attachment   The avowed object of exercise of power under section 83 for the purpose of provisional attachment of any property is to protect the interest of the Revenue.Ultimately, if sufficient material surfaces indicating the involvement of the writ-applicant in some bogus transaction, the next step in the process can always be a show-cause notice under section 73 or Section 74 of the Act, as the case may be. However, to provisionally attach all the bank accounts and that too those accounts in which there is hardly any balance would only cause undue hardship to the assessee   An order of provisional attachment cannot be as a matter of course. It is one of the drastic measures which the authority may be compelled to take if the situation demands for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government Revenue.   When there are plethora of judgments explaining Section 83 in details, then why so much of litigation in the High Court. The only reason that can be attributed is the mechanical exercise of power under section 83 of the Act. This should stop at the earliest.   Union of India as well as CBDT were directed to issue appropriate instructions or guidelines at the earliest with respect to the exercise of power under section 83
