1 [

Provisional attachment of property

159 . (1) Where the Commissioner decides to attach any property, including bank account in accordance with the provisions of section 83, he shall pass an order in FORM GST DRC-22 to that effect mentioning therein, the details of property which is attached.

(2) The Commissioner shall send a copy of the order of attachment to the concerned Revenue Authority or Transport Authority or any such Authority to place encumbrance on the said movable or immovable property, which shall be removed only on the written instructions from the Commissioner to that effect.

(3) Where the property attached is of perishable or hazardous nature, and if the taxable person pays an amount equivalent to the market price of such property or the amount that is or may become payable by the taxable person, whichever is lower, then such property shall be released forthwith, by an order in FORM GST DRC-23, on proof of payment.

(4) Where the taxable person fails to pay the amount referred to in sub-rule (3) in respect of the said property of perishable or hazardous nature, the Commissioner may dispose of such property and the amount realized thereby shall be adjusted against the tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount payable by the taxable person.

(5) Any person whose property is attached may, within seven days of the attachment under sub-rule (1), file an objection to the effect that the property attached was or is not liable to attachment, and the Commissioner may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to the person filing the objection, release the said property by an order in FORM GST DRC- 23.

(6) The Commissioner may, upon being satisfied that the property was, or is no longer liable for attachment, release such property by issuing an order in FORM GST DRC- 23.]

following detailed audit checklist covering the above aspects for the audit of bank balances, based on SA 505 External Confirmations, PCAOB's AS 2310 The Auditor's Use of Confirmation (effective for FYE on or after 6/15/2025) (hereinafter referred to as "AS 2310(New)"), Guidance Note on Audit of Cash and Bank Balances, relevant provisions of Companies Act,2013 and Income-Tax Act,1961, and case laws.

| Sr. No. | Particulars | Yes/No /NA | W.P. Ref. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I. | Features of Bank balances that impact related Audit procedures |  |  |
| (1) | Have you factored in the inherent nature of Bank balances-that they are highly fraud-prone? |  |  |
| II. | Audit Objectives |  |  |
| (2) | Have you noted that the audit objective for the audit of Bank balances is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in support of the following assertions: Existence: that recorded bank balances exist at the year-end Rights: that recorded bank balances represent the assets of the entity Cut-off: Banking transactions are recorded in the period in which they take place and not earlier/later[See Barings Plc v Coopers & Lybrand(a firm) & Ors [2003] EWHC 1319 (Ch)] Completeness: there are no unrecorded bank balances. Valuation: in certain special cases–e.g. Foreign currency held by the entity/bank accounts designated in foreign currencies. |  |  |
| III | Risk Assessment |  |  |
| (1) | Have you assessed the risks of the entity not disclosing all bank balances in accounts either due to lack of awareness or deliberately with the intent to reduce the income-tax liability? |  |  |
| (2) | Have you assessed the risks of window-dressing of the year-end Current ratio by showing payments to trade creditors as at 31st March by dating the cheques 31st March but delivering /sending them to creditors after a time lag (say at April end/May)? |  |  |
| (3) | Have you assessed the risks of cheques dated 31st March and shown as payments to MSE Suppliers but being handed over to them much later to circumvent the provisions of disallowance of late payment to MSEs under Section 43B(h) of the Income-Tax Act,1961? |  |  |
| (4) | Have you assessed the risks that the cheques to MSE Suppliers are dated on the due date for payment under section 15 of MSMED Act but handed over/delivered to them after a big time lag so as to show payments within the due date, avoid disallowance under Section 43b(h) of Income-Tax Act,1961, and avoid provisioning for and payment of interest on delayed payments under Section 16 of MSMED Act? |  |  |
| (5) | Have you assessed the risks that vendor masters will be updated with fake Udyam Numbers given by Suppliers without validating them on the Udyam Portal by employees conniving with suppliers so that the system treats them as Micro or Small Enterprises (MSEs) and pays them on priority as MSEs? |  |  |
| (6) | Have you presumed the existence of the risks of management override of internal controls by use of pre-signed blank cheques by the promoter of the entity for diversion of funds to him and his family members by using group entities as conduits as was the case in CA Lavitha Shetty, In re [2023] 151 taxmann.com 526 (NFRA)? [See SA 240] |  |  |
| (7) | Have you assessed the risks of the entity accounting for cheques dated 31st March but received thereafter as cheques on hand either to window-dress current ratio or to show lower related party balances or to evergreen loans to related parties? |  |  |
| (8) | Have you assessed the risks of fraud committed on the entity through internet banking frauds, hacking, etc? |  |  |
| (9) | Have you assessed the risks of fraud committed on the entity by fraudulent encashment of cheques? |  |  |
| (9A) | (a) Does the entity maintain too many bank accounts that are not warranted by its size? (b) Have you exercised greater care in satisfying yourself about the genuineness of the transactions and balance? |  |  |
| IV | Internal Control Evaluation |  |  |
| (10) | Have you evaluated the following aspects of internal controls over bank balances and banking transactions of the entity: (a) Segregation of duties relating to; authorisation of transactions. issuance of cheques. writing books of accounts (b) Proper authorisation of banking transactions (c) Restrictive crossing of cheques (d) Whether the entity had availed Positive Pay facility to protect against fraudulent encashment of cheques (e) Per day limits set on Internet banking transactions (f) Per day limits set on UPI transactions (g) Periodic reconciliation of bank balances. (h) Safe custody of cheque books, internet banking passwords etc |  |  |
| (11) | Is a record maintained of all cheques issued and cancelled cheques not detached from the cheque book? |  |  |
| (12) | Does the entity have any system of pre-signed blank cheques being issued to anyone? |  |  |
| (13) | Is there a proper accounting control over cheques received through cheques on hand account right from the time they are received to the time they are banked till they are credited by the bank on realisation? |  |  |
| (14) | (a) Is it ensured that cheques received other than post dated cheques are debited to cheques on hand account on receipt and then to bank account when deposited and deposit is evidenced by pay-in slip? (b) Is it ensured that there is no direct debit to the bank account on receipt of a cheque? |  |  |
| (15) | Are Cheques on hand accounts reviewed from time to time to inquire about items outstanding in it as to why they have not been banked or, if banked, why it is still outstanding, and what is the status of the realisation of the cheque? |  |  |
| (16) | Are entries passed in bank accounts on a daily basis, a Bank Reconciliation Statement prepared as at every month end, and necessary action taken on items appearing in BRS? Note: In the case of companies, accounting for receipts and payments on a day-to-day basis is a requirement of Section 338(2) of the Companies Act,2013. In the case of other entities, it is a sound and prudent practice to ensure internal control over bank balances. |  |  |
| (16A) | Does the entity ensure to cross cheques received as "account payee" if not already so crossed by the party before banking them especially if the amount is Rs. 2,00,000 or more (Section 269ST of Income-Tax Act,1961)? |  |  |
| (16B) | Does the entity ensure to cross cheques as account payee before issuing them?[See Sections 40A(3), 269T, Section 43(1)] |  |  |
| V | Audit Trail |  |  |
| (17) | In case of a Company using an accounting software to maintain books of account, have you verified the following regarding the audit trail for updating vendor master records: Non-Configurable: The audit trail feature must be non-configurable. That is to say, the audit trail should not be capable of being disabled and should not be capable of being tampered with,. Enabled throughout the year: Verify whether the audit trail feature was enabled/ operated throughout the year. Auditor's responsibility is limited to transactions that have been recorded in the accounting software and subsequent changes made to those transactions- whether all transactions recorded in the software are covered in the audit trail feature? Proviso to Rule 3(1) of Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014 prescribes the requirement of an audit trail only in the context of books of account by stating that accounting software should be capable of creating an edit log of "each change made in books of account." The auditor's responsibilities have been prescribed for "all transactions recorded in the software." Accordingly, the auditor's responsibility under Rule 11(g) is restricted to transactions which have been recorded in the accounting software and subsequent changes made to those transactions (which is demonstrated through rectification/ additional entities). Compliance with statutory record retention requirements: Has the audit trail been preserved as per statutory requirements for record retention under Section 128(5) of the Companies Act,2013? |  |  |
| VI | Completeness of disclosure of all bank balances |  |  |
| (18) | Have you verified AIS (Annual Information Statement) and Form 26AS generated by the Income-Tax Department? |  |  |
| (19) | (a) Have you verified bank accounts reflected in previous year's ITR filed by the entity? (b) Are all those bank accounts disclosed in the balance sheet of the year under audit? |  |  |
| VII | Bank balance |  |  |
| (20) | a. Is the bank balance in the books a debit balance? b. If the bank balance in the books is a credit balance, is there an overdraft arrangement with the bank? c. If there is no overdraft arrangement with the bank and the bank account shows a credit balance, have you treated it as a red flag and enquired into the reasons?[See CA Lavitha Shetty, In re [2023] 151 taxmann.com 526] |  |  |
| VIII | Cut-off: Accounting for cheques received/other receipts through the bank in the proper period |  |  |
| (21) | Post Dated Cheques Verify that PDCs received have not been accounted for as deposits in bank account Verify that PDCs received are not accounted as cheques on hand |  |  |
| (22) | Cheques received other than PDCs Have you verified the composition of balance of cheques on hand account? Have you verified that it does not include PDCs received? Have you verified that cheques received, which are dated 31st March or earlier but received after 31st March, are not included in cheques on hand in the balance sheet as at 31st March? |  |  |
| (23) | Have you ensured that cheques dated 31st March or before are not accounted as payments if handed over/delivered after 31st March? |  |  |
| (24) | Have you ensured that credit received in the bank account in the next accounting period is not accounted for as a receipt in the current accounting period?[See Barings Plc v Coopers & Lybrand(a firm) & Ors [2003] EWHC 1319 (Ch)] |  |  |
| IX | Existence of bank balances :Direct Confirmation/External Confirmation Procedure |  |  |
| (25) | Have you factored in mandatory requirements of PCAOB's AS 2310 The Auditor's Use of Confirmation (effective for FYE on or after 6/15/2025) (hereinafter referred to as "AS 2310(New)") which provides that for cash and cash equivalents held by third parties ("cash"), the auditor should perform confirmation procedures or otherwise obtain relevant and reliable audit evidence by directly accessing information maintained by a knowledgeable external source.? Note: The above requirement seems to be a case of Regulators learning from the Satyam case. |  |  |
| (26) | (a) Have you Advised the entity to send letters of request to all its bankers to confirm the balances directly to the auditor? (b) Do the requests for confirmation also cover dormant accounts and accounts closed during the year under audit? |  |  |
| X | Examination of Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) |  |  |
| (27) | (a) Have you verified that cheques issued by the entity but not presented for payment, cheques deposited for collection but not credited, have been debited/credited in the subsequent period? (b) Have you examined the bank statement for the relevant period to confirm this? |  |  |
| (28) | Where entries for payment have been made in the books of account for cheques issued before the year-end, but these cheques were delivered to the parties only after the year-end, have you verified that the entity has reversed the entries? |  |  |
| (29) | (a) Have you paid special attention to those items in the BRS that are outstanding for an unduly long period? (b) Have you ascertained the reasons for such items from the management? (c) Have you examined whether such items require any adjustment or write-off? |  |  |

1. Section 45 of Gujarat Value Added Tax Act (GVAT Act) deals with provisional attachment. As per the said section, if during the pendency of any proceedings of assessment or reassessment of turnover escaping assessment, if Commissioner is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of revenue it is necessary to attach the property of a dealer, he may by order in writing attach provisionally any property belonging to the dealer. Property can be provisionally attached for a maximum period of one year. Rule 41 of Gujarat Value Added Tax Rules, 2005 (GVAT Rules) provides that Commissioner has to pass an order mentioning the details of property that is attached. If the property attached is of immovable nature, he shall send intimation to the land revenue authority to endorse a charge on said property. If the property is of a perishable nature, provisionally attached property shall be immediately released on payment of the market price of said property. If the dealer fails to pay the same, Commissioner shall dispose of such property and adjust the amount realized against the tax liability. Thus only condition required to be satisfied before making provisional attachment is formation of an opinion that in order to protect the interest of revenue, attachment is needed. 3.2 Additional authentication by a trusted person for high-value digital transactions by vulnerable sections of society

Certain sections of society, such as citizens above a certain age or differently-abled persons (persons with disabilities), may be particularly vulnerable to social engineering–based frauds. Such frauds often involve impersonating family members or fabricating urgent scenarios involving medical, legal, or other emergencies.

These targeted incidents frequently result in disproportionately higher financial losses, underscoring the need to consider enhanced protective measures for this customer segment, alongside sustained awareness initiatives.

Accordingly, the RBI has proposed that such measures be made mandatory for citizens aged 70 years and above and persons with disabilities, while remaining optional for all other individual customers. This approach seeks to ensure tailored protection for those at higher risk of fraud or exploitation due to age or disability, while allowing flexibility for the broader customer base.

The proposed safeguard mechanism may take the form of a “trusted person” designated by a vulnerable customer. This trusted individual would act as an additional layer of authentication for high-value transactions, such as those exceeding Rs 50,000.

Notably, nearly 92% of the value of frauds reported on the NCRP exceeds this limit. Thus, the threshold balances operational efficiency for smaller transactions with strong protection for higher-value transfers.

Any change of a trusted person may be permitted only after a mandatory 24-hour cooling-off period, thereby ensuring that such decisions are deliberate and informed.

Further, vulnerable customers may be allowed to opt out of the safeguard mechanism after a 24-hour cooling-off period from the time of request. Banks would be required to clearly explain the associated risks to the customer before processing such requests, thereby ensuring informed decision-making.

The proposal to introduce additional authentication through a trusted person for high-value transactions aims to strengthen protection for vulnerable sections of society against fraud. It would reduce the risk of financial loss arising from social engineering scams while promoting informed decision-making. At the same time, the optional framework for other users ensures flexibility without imposing unnecessary restrictions. As part of the KYC process, banks are required to obtain supporting documents regarding the nature of the customer’s business and their financial status. Banking is the only industry that directly deals in cash and cash is susceptible to fraud. Therefore, the Banking industry evolved unique features to work smoothly with safeguards from fraud. Statutory branch audit is the part of those safeguards. This article throws light on the concept of statutory branch audit of the banks and discusses about the unique features of functioning of Bank branches, functions to be performed by the auditors, etc. The author, here, has suggested some practical steps to be taken by the auditor immediately on receipt of appointment letter and opines that proper planning and knowledge of relevant law are the most essential things for proper and fruitful conduct and completion of Bank Branch audits

Introduction

Banking is the only industry that directly deals in money, whereas other sectors of industry be it manufacturing or service sector get cash after selling their respective products or rendering services. And cash is most susceptible to fraud. Therefore, banking industry evolved unique features to work smoothly with safeguards from fraud. Statutory audit is part of those safeguards. Thus, to properly understand the Bank Branch Audit, the uniqueness of functioning of Bank Branches is to be understood

Uniqueness of functioning of bank branches

2. The unique features of functioning of bank branches are as under :

(i ) The first unique thing about bank branches is that they do not comply with any statutory change howsoever well publicized it may be, unless there is a circular from their own head office. When TDS provisions for rent were introduced, the bank branches did not start deducting TDS until circulars from Head Office (H.O.) to this effect were issued, though branches of companies had started deducting this tax after passage of the relevant Finance Act. Why is it so ? This tradition of doing things only as per H.O. instructions has deve-loped due to the years of experience by Banking Industry in our country. As the branches of banks are scattered geographically, in the interest of security and standardization, procedures for handling banking transactions are laid out elaborately in operating manuals and whatever changes are required to be made in these operations, are carried out through H.O. circulars. Therefore, Branch Auditors have to go through all these operating manuals and circulars meticulously.

(ii ) The second unique feature of functioning of bank branches and for that matter ‘Banks ’ in general is that banks record their books on principle of triple entry instead of double entry. This system of recording their transactions on triple entry basis ensures internal control in the functioning of bank branches and this system is so important for banks that even in computerized recording system in banks this system is religiously followed. The triple entry system is executed by recording all vouchers in General Ledger (GL) in addition to recording of these vouchers in their respective accounts.

For example, when we deposit in or withdraw from our savings account any amount, the entry passed by the Bank Branch is not only in our saving account but also in G.L. and thus, the total of all savings accounts should tally with the total of savings in G.L. In the manual era of accounting, two separate persons were entrusted with the work of writing G.L. and other books. In computerized accounting, however, the writing is done by computer. But still G.L., is thought to be indispensable as it is strong tool of internal control.

(iii ) The third unique thing about bank branches is that whereas in other sectors we may have Internal Audit in addition to the statutory audit, in case of Banks besides statutory audit there are RBI Audit, Revenue Audit, Concurrent Audit, Internal Inspection and nowadays another new audit, i.e., system audit. Thus, round the year there is some or other audit going on in Bank Branches.

(iv ) The fourth unique feature about bank branches is that all bank branches whether small or big have to strictly follow the procedure of half yearly closing. There is no relaxation in this regard in Banking Industry.

(v ) The fifth unique features about Bank Branches is that every Branch has to have externally strong control system. If an auditor finds any laxity in this respect, he must be very alert. Every Bank Branch as earlier told, has to maintain G.L. and this G.L. has to be balanced in form of GLB i.e., General Ledger Balance Book. The GLB contains the assets and liabilities of the branch and when tallied indicates correct balancing. The GLB needs to be tallied by the next morning of the transactions of the previous day. This is the case in the most of efficient branches but in average branches also four days delay in tallying GLB is considered normal if the branch follows manual system. However, in case of computerized branches, GLB should invariably be tallied next day.

In case of CST v. Sri Jagatbandhu Mohanty, [1961] 12 STC 706, the Orissa High Court said that there are two important points of difference between the Bihar Sales Tax Act and the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. (1) Whereas income-tax for the assessment year is assessed on the income of the previous year, sales tax becomes liable to be paid immediately after each sale is effected though, for facility of computation and payment of tax, provision has been made for the filing of returns at the. expiry of each quarter. (2) Whereas rates of income-tax vary in accordance with the amount of income and therefore no one can be certain of what income-tax he has to pay at least until the accounting year expires, the rate of sales tax does not vary on the amount of taxable turnover and a dealer, therefore, can always be certain of what sales tax he has to pay as soon as he effects a sale. In other words, sales tax becomes payable immediately after a sale is transacted. It said further that the words 'due' and 'payable' are separate. Eventually, honourable high court came to the conclusion that it is, therefore, clear that to the extent of liability admitted in a return the amount of tax is payable before the dealer submits that return. Thus, there is no doubt that the tax is payable since the sale is transacted and it is incumbent upon the registered dealer to state that amount in the return when submitted.

(ii) Is there any threshold limit for invoking attachment provision ? - Neither section 73C nor the Rules lay down any threshold limit for initiating attachment proceedings. However, the CBEC’s Circular No. 103/06/2008-ST, dated July 1, 2008, provides that it should be resorted to only in a case where the service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakh.

(iii) Against whom can the provisions of attachment be invoked ? - As per section 73C, provisional attachment can be ordered in respect of any property belonging to a person on whom a notice has been served under section 73(1) or 73A(3). It may be noted that under section 73(1), a notice can be served on the person chargeable with the service tax which has not been levied or paid or which has been short-levied or short-paid or the person to whom service tax has been erroneously refunded, whereas, a notice under section 73A(3) can be served on - (1) a person liable to pay service tax who has collected any amount in excess of the service tax assessed or determined and paid on any taxable service from the recipient of the taxable service, or (2) any person who has collected any amount as service tax, which is not required to be collected, from any other person.

(iv) Which property can be attached under the provision of service tax ? - As noted in FAQ 3, provisional attachment under section 73C can be ordered in respect of any ‘property’ belonging to the specified person. Rule 2(c) of the Rules defines the term ‘property’ to include immovable property. Further, rule 4(2) of the Rules provides that movable property shall be attached only if the immovable property is not sufficient to protect the interest of revenue.

The CBEC, vide its circular dated July 1, 2008, has clarified that immovable property/properties which is/are used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached.

(v) Can personal property(ies) of proprietor/partner(s)/ director(s) be also attached ? - As per proviso to rule 3(3) of the Rules, personal property of proprietor or partners or directors, as the case may be, shall not be attached. As per rule 2(d), ‘personal property’ means any movable or immovable property belonging to a proprietor or partner or director, which is not in relation to business activity.

Accordingly, the CBEC in its circular dated July 1, 2008 has also clarified that any movable or immovable property which is in personal use of the sole proprietor/partner/director cannot be attached.

(vi) What shall be the extent of attachment ? - In terms of rule 4(1), the provisional attachment of property shall be to the extent it requires to protect the interest of revenue. In other words, the value of property attached shall be as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of ‘pending revenue’.

The term ‘pending revenue’ is defined under rule 2(b) to mean "any service tax that has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A". Thus, the term ‘pending revenue’ refers to the amount demanded in the proceedings under section 73 or 73A.

(vii) What can be the possible justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary ? - If the Central Excise Officer reasonably believes that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, any of his property(ies) liable to attachment, it can be considered as sufficient justification necessitating attachment of property. The belief must, however, be based on substantial grounds.

(viii) What precautions should the Central Excise Officer take before initiating attachment proceedings ? - Although section 73C and the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, are both silent in this regard, the CBEC has in its circular dated July 1, 2008, stated emphatically that the remedy of attachment is of extraordinary nature and should be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. There should be sufficient justification to hold the view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The Central Excise Officer should, in his proposal for attachment, clearly state the grounds on which he entertains the reasonable belief that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any.

The circular further states that appropriate disciplinary action shall be initiated against the officers who may be found to have exercised the powers of provisional attachment of property frivolously and without sound reasons.

Extension of Inverted Duty Structure (IDS) refund to 'input services' and 'capital goods'

Section 54(3) of the CGST Act, read with Rule 89(5) of the CGST Rules, prescribes the mechanism for granting refunds of unutilised input tax credit (ITC) arising from an inverted duty structure. However, the statutory formula restricts the scope of 'Net ITC' exclusively to input tax credit availed on input goods, explicitly excluding input services and capital goods from the refund computation.

As a result, taxpayers operating under an inverted tax structure accumulate substantial unutilised ITC on account of input services (such as job work, freight, utilities, professional services, etc.) and capital goods, which remain permanently blocked. While large enterprises are generally able to absorb such accumulation due to diversified product portfolios and higher-rated outward supplies, MSMEs and smaller manufacturers, particularly those engaged in single-product or low-margin businesses, face severe working capital constraints due to the non-refundability of such credits.

The adverse impact of this restriction has been further exacerbated by recent GST rate rationalisation measures, which have reduced output tax rates without a corresponding alignment of input tax rates, intensifying inverted duty structures across several sectors.

In this context, it is recommended that the refund mechanism under Rule 89(5) be suitably amended to include input services and capital goods within the scope of 'Net ITC' for the purpose of inverted duty structure refunds. Such a measure would align the refund framework with the fundamental GST principle of tax neutrality, prevent tax cascading, and significantly improve liquidity, thereby promoting ease of doing business and enhancing manufacturing competitiveness.

67. IDS refunds should be allowed for inputs and outputs at the same GST rate

Under Section 54 of the CGST Act, taxpayers are entitled to claim refunds for accumulated input tax credit on account of an inverted duty structure (IDS), i.e., where the rate of tax on inputs exceeds the rate of tax on outward supplies. However, tax authorities have often denied refunds under Section 54(3) read with Rule 89 of the CGST Rules, where the input tax rate on certain goods exceeds the output tax rate, even when the principal input and output attract the same GST rate. This has created uncertainty and impacted cash flow for businesses.

Recent judicial developments indicate a more purposive interpretation of the IDS provisions. In Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs. Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax [2025] 174.taxmann.com 1 (Karnataka), the Karnataka High Court observed that an IDS refund cannot be denied merely because some inputs are taxed at a higher rate than the output, so long as the principal input and the outward supply attract the same GST rate and the accumulation of ITC is otherwise attributable to the rate structure.

Further, during the 56th GST Council meeting, the government indicated its intent to simplify IDS refund processes, hinting at regulatory changes in the near future. Taxpayers can anticipate a more streamlined and predictable mechanism for claiming IDS refunds, potentially reducing litigation and enhancing liquidity management.

68. Blocking of the electronic credit ledger with zero or negative ITC may be reviewed

Rule 86A of the CGST Rules was inserted videNotification No. 75/2019- Central Tax, dated 26-12-2019, empowering the GST authorities to restrict the utilisation of ITC in the ECL under exceptional circumstances.

In practice, instances have been observed where tax authorities have blocked the ECL on a negative basis, i.e., restricted utilisation of ITC in excess of the balance actually available in the ECL at the time of passing the order. Such negative blocking effectively prevents utilisation of future credits, leading to severe cash-flow constraints for taxpayers, particularly during audits or verification proceedings.

Recently, the Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue's Special Leave Petition in Kings Security Guard Services (P.) Ltd. 174 taxmann.com 982, thereby affirming the decision of the Delhi High Court. The High Court, relying on its earlier ruling in Best Crop Science (P.) Ltd. [2024] 166 taxmann.com 654, held that Rule 86A of CGST Rules is not a machinery provision for recovery of tax or dues under CGST Act but an emergent measure for protection of revenue by temporarily not allowing debit of available ITC in ECL order disallowing debit from ECL, in excess of ITC available in ECL at the time of passing the order.

In view of the above judicial pronouncements, it is recommended that the scope and application of Rule 86A of the CGST Rules be reviewed and clarified to prevent its use as a recovery mechanism. However, appropriate safeguards may continue to be retained to allow restriction of ITC utilisation in genuine cases involving fraud or wilful misuse of input tax credit, subject to due process and statutory limitations.

Committing fraud is a difficult task, and the majority of astute employees will refrain from concealing their crimes if they believe internal controls are lax and they can get away with it. However, if managers monitor employees regularly, employees may be forced to fabricate documents to support their irregular transactions when committing fraud. That requires more dedication than some employees are willing to provide, which is why adding a simple control, such as the business owner reviewing the bank reconciliation statements, acts as an effective deterrent.

CONCLUSION

A bank reconciliation is used to compare the organizational records to those of the banks to determine if any discrepancies exist between the two sets of cash and banking transactions. The book balance is the ending balance of the cash records from the organization's perspective, whereas the bank balance is the ending balance of the bank's version. It is ubiquitous for the two balances to differ, which one should investigate and adjust in its records. If these differences are ignored, significant discrepancies will eventually develop. As a result, the bank account may become overdrawn, cheques may bounce, and the organization may incur various overdraft fees. In some instances, the bank may even choose to close the account.

Additionally, bank reconciliation is beneficial to determine whether any customer cheques have bounced or if any issued cheques have been altered or even stolen and cashed without knowledge. Thus, completing a bank reconciliation is critical for detecting fraud. When a search for fraudulent transactions is ongoing, daily bank account reconciliation may be necessary to obtain an early warning of a problem. When the annual audit comes around, the auditors will always examine the company's final bank reconciliation as part of their testing procedures, which is another reason to complete reconciliation.

77. Allow small-scale ice cream manufacturers to opt for a composition scheme

The GST law allows certain taxpayers with turnover up to Rs. 1.5 Crores to opt for a composition scheme, which enables them to pay GST at lower rates and comply with fewer compliance requirements. However, this scheme is not available to all taxpayers as the law provides a specific restriction for a list of persons who cannot opt to pay tax under the composition scheme. This list includes manufacturers of Pan Masala, Tobacco, Ice Cream, and other edible items. This restriction was introduced based on the recommendation of the 17th GST Council meeting.

Small-scale ice cream manufacturers have criticised this restriction, arguing that ice cream has been placed on par with Pan Masala and Tobacco without adequate justification. They contend that ice cream is a widely consumed item and should not be arbitrarily classified as sin goods without proper reasoning.

Recently, this issue came before the Chhattisgarh High Court, wherein the Hon'ble Court directed17 of the GST Council to reconsider the exclusion of small-scale ice cream manufacturers from the composition scheme. The Court highlighted that the GST Council had provided no specific reason to exclude Ice Cream Manufacturers from the benefit of the composition scheme, and it should have considered the socio-economic impact of placing ice cream in the 18% tax rate. A similar order was earlier passed by Delhi High Court18 on the same matter.

It is recommended that provisions relating to the composition scheme should be suitably amended to allow its benefit to Ice Cream manufacturers.

78. Include Petroleum Products, ATF, and Natural gas under GST

The GST Council's 45th meeting, held on September 17, 2021, discussed including petroleum products in the GST framework. Although the Council deferred the decision, there is growing consensus on gradually bringing petroleum products under GST. Aviation Turbine Fuel ('ATF') and Natural Gas stand out as potential candidates for phased inclusion due to their distinct characteristics. The inclusion of ATF and natural gas under GST can significantly benefit both sectors and pave the way for the broader inclusion of other petroleum products. A well-planned, phased approach will ensure a simplified, uniform tax structure aligned with global best practices.

79. Rationalise GST rates

The GST structure in India currently includes multiple tax slabs of 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%, with certain products also attracting a compensation cess over and above the GST rate. Over the years, there has been consistent dialogue about simplifying this structure, primarily by reducing the number of tax rates. One proposed reform is to merge the 12% and 18% slabs into a single, moderate rate. The multiple GST rates add layers of complexity to the tax system, creating compliance challenges for businesses, especially for MSMEs. With varying rates for different products and services, businesses face challenges in determining the correct tax slab for their offerings, leading to disputes and litigations. Consolidating GST rates, especially the proposed merger of the 12% and 18% slabs into a single GST rate, can significantly simplify India's tax system.

Following table summarize common reconciliation discrepancies in GST Reconciliations & Suggested Auditor Actions: The Value Addition Principle and GST Payment Patterns:

Value addition principle suggests that consistent Goods and Services Tax (GST) payments made through banking channels typically signify that a company is adding value within its supply chain. When a business procures goods or services, it pays GST (Input Tax Credit - ITC), and when it sells its products or services, it collects GST on the value added. The net GST paid (Output GST minus eligible ITC) reflects this value addition. Regular and substantial GST payments often correlate with genuine business activity and value creation.

However, auditors must approach this principle with a degree of nuance. While a strong indicator, the link between GST payments and value addition is not always direct or simplistic. Several legitimate business factors can influence GST payment patterns, such as the entity's industry, business model, capital expenditure cycles, and specific GST provisions like inverted duty structures. Therefore, while GST payment patterns provide a valuable starting point for analysis, they must be interpreted within the broader context of the company's operations and the prevailing economic environment.

Certain red flags emerging from the relationship between GST payment patterns and profitability may reveal unexpected business or compliance trends not immediately evident from the financial statements. Key red flags include:

-

High GST payments accompanied by poor profit margins: This scenario could suggest issues such as inflated input costs, inefficient operations, or even the possibility of sales suppression where output tax is paid on reported sales, but the actual profitability is eroded by unrecorded transactions or expenses.

-

Minimal GST payments despite substantial reported profits: This might indicate legitimate scenarios like high non-GST expenses (e.g., salaries, depreciation, interest), significant export sales (which are zero-rated), or operations under an inverted duty structure. However, it could also point to potential issues like suppressed sales, inflated or fictitious ITC claims, or misclassification of supplies as exempt or non-GST.

-

Sudden fluctuations in GST payments without corresponding changes in revenue: Such volatility could be due to seasonal business factors, bulk purchases leading to higher ITC in certain periods, or large, infrequent sales. However, if unexplained, it could also indicate inconsistent reporting or manipulation of tax liabilities.

-

GST payments significantly lower than industry benchmarks for similar turnover: While industry benchmarks must be used cautiously due to variations in business models, a persistent and significant deviation can be an indicator requiring further exploration.

It is crucial to understand that these red flags are not, in themselves, conclusive evidence of wrongdoing. Instead, they serve as indicators of potential financial stress, operational inefficiencies, compliance gaps, or, in some instances, fraudulent activity. The auditor's role is to investigate the underlying reasons for these patterns through detailed substantive testing and inquiries with management.

Key Questions by Statutory Auditors for above Red Flags:

To effectively "connect the dots," auditors should pose insightful questions to management. There are few sets of questions categorized by operational area, which serve as an excellent framework for auditors:

-

On Asset Acquisition:

o

"Has the company made significant capital asset purchases in the period that could explain the high input tax credits?" (This helps ascertain if high ITC is due to genuine capital investment or other reasons).

o

"Can you reconcile the timing of input tax credits claimed with the capitalization schedule?" (This verifies the linkage between asset acquisition and ITC claims).

-

On Duty Structure:

o

"Is the company operating in a sector with inverted duty structure? How does this impact your net GST liability?" (Understanding this is key to explaining potentially low net GST payments despite turnover).

o

"What steps has management taken to address working capital blockage due to inverted duty structure? How is the deficit in working capital getting managed?" (This delves into financial management aspects arising from GST structure).

o

Regarding cash credit facilities, auditors should inquire if GST receivables are appropriately considered in drawing power calculations, especially if they include higher taxes on inputs that might be part of an inverted duty structure.

-

On Cost Structure:

o

"What percentage of your total costs are non-GST applicable expenses like employee costs, finance cost and depreciation?" (High non-GST costs can explain lower net GST payments relative to profits).

o

"How do your non-creditable expenses compare to industry benchmarks?" (This helps assess the reasonableness of such expenses).

-

On Credits and Other Compliance:

o

"Can you provide aging analysis of unutilized input tax credits?" and "Analyse the movement in such aging to know the reasons for credit accumulation." (This helps identify slow-moving or obsolete ITC, or potential issues with refund claims).

o

"How does the company handle GST on exports and exempt supplies? Are proper refunds being claimed?" (Ensures compliance with specific provisions related to zero-rated and exempt supplies).

C. Business related

For any taxpayer, one of the most important aspects is to analyse their business organisation and plan accordingly before migrating into the GST to avoid any unwanted situations. The following examples explain this.

More than one unit (same business vertical) in the same state: Currently, under the VAT regime, a company can have more than one registration in a State. There are no restrictions in obtaining and maintaining more than one VAT registration. However, under the GST, a company can opt for state wise single registration i.e., single registration for all places of business in a state. If a taxpayer opts for separate registrations i.e., different registrations for different units in the same State under GST (if permitted by the jurisdictional authority), it will pay GST on movements of goods between two units. Although the same would be creditable to the recipient, it would lead to blockage of funds. Therefore, while migrating into GST, the taxpayer should take a considered decision whether they should take a state-wise single registration covering all units or take unit-wise multiple registrations.

More than one unit (different business verticals) in the same state: Under the GST regime, section 23 of the revised model GST law provides an option to opt for separate registrations for each business vertical in a State. The taxpayer must clearly identify the business verticals as per the definition of "business verticals". It may be noted that it is upon the decision of the taxpayer to obtain single or multiple registrations for different business verticals. This would also have an impact on the unutilized credit pertaining to each business vertical.

Subsidies: If a taxpayer has two units in a State of which one unit is new and is currently enjoying State incentives/ subsidies, whereas, there are no such incentives/ subsidies for other unit. Currently, the taxpayer has obtained separate VAT registration for each unit. Under the GST regime, the taxpayer has to understand that whether the subsidies/ incentives would be available for single registration or not. For taxpayers who have already migrated as a single registration in a State, in such situations the taxpayer may have to re-examine their registrations once there is some clarity on this aspect.

Merger/ De-merger/ Slump sale: In case a taxpayer has business plans for merger/ de-merger/ slump sale in the near future, the registrations of business units should be done keeping in mind the proposed plan.

Many more business aspects need to be considered before migrating into the GST, which depends on a case-to-case basis. The taxpayer should look into it before taking any decision on the migration of existing registrations into GST. Simultaneously, the taxpayer has to keep in mind the due dates specified for migration of various categories of registrants in the released enrolment schedule.

Upon successful verification, the GST portal system shall generate an acknowledgement containing the acknowledgement receipt number (ARN) within 15 minutes of submission. This number should be stored as it is proof that the taxpayer has successfully migrated and all future communications/ tracking of status shall be sent/ done using the ARN number.

Fixed Assets and Costs of Inventories Apart from impacting the chartered accountants in discharging their functions, GST has also impacted financial reporting. One of the key changes that GST has brought is reduced capitalisation of indirect taxes, thereby increasing the profits. This change has benefitted industries which had large capitalisation of fixed assets. The credit for certain indirect taxes was either not admissible or was allowed subject to fulfilment of certain conditions. With the advent of GST, credit for all kinds of indirect taxes is admissible, thereby reducing capitalisation of fixed assets and boosting the profit margins.

Similarly, the cost of the inventories has reduced as input tax credit is available on both goods and services. On the other hand, stock transfers which are treated akin to sale, leads to increase in inventory costs as every branch has a separate GST registration and a GSTIN and GST is attracted for every stock transfer.

Seamless Transition to GST - Carry Forward of Input Tax Credit

Another special feature of GST is smooth carry forward of the amount of input credit remaining unutilised as per the previous indirect tax laws. However, such carry forward is allowed subject to fulfilment of certain conditions. For instance, carry forward of unutilised CENVAT credit is not allowed if the person has not furnished returns required under the previous laws, for a period of 6 months immediately preceding July 1, 2017.

Changes in Chart of Accounts - Reduced Number of Ledger Accounts

As the introduction of GST has subsumed all indirect tax levies, large organisations using SAP or ERP for accounting have a big challenge underway. General Ledger Coding post implementation of GSTacts as a key challenge for these companies. The number of GL codes in the previous indirect tax structure used to be high as compared to the new taxation regime owing to the taxation provisions. For example, CENVAT credit on Capital Goods was allowed in two instalments of 50% each accordingly, there were two GL Codes namely CENVAT Credit on Capital Goods and Deferred CENVAT Credit on Capital Goods. Going forward, there is no such concept of deferment, instead full credit can be availed in the year of purchase of Capital Goods. Thus, GL Codes of large organisations need to be updated with careful planning and understanding.

Corporates and business, not only in India but around the world are keenly observing its impact and how it unfolds in the coming months. Its still early days and the real impact of the new Act is yet to be seen. One can only hope that it will prove to be a boon for businesses in the longer run and will go to make the lives of accountants and auditors simpler as well.

69. Rationalisation of formula for calculation of refund in case of export under CIF contract is made without payment of tax

Section 54(3) of the CGST Act, 2017 provides for the refund of the balance of ITC where export is made without payment of tax under bond or letter of undertaking. Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017 provides the refund formula for the same as under:

Refund amount = [(Turnover of zero-rated supply of goods + Turnover of zero-rated supply of services)/Adjusted total turnover] * Net ITC

In the given formula, regarding the turnover of the zero-rated supply of goods, the Explanation to Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules30 provides that the value of goods exported out of India would be taken as lower of the following values:

(a)

Free on Board (FOB) value declared in the Shipping Bill or Bill of Export form, as the case may be; or

(b)

The value is declared in the tax invoice or bill of supply.

Notably, for the export of goods under CIF contracts, the exporter has to separately report the FOB value of goods, insurance and freight expenses in the shipping bill. The FOB value reported in the shipping bill would always be less than the value as per the tax invoice. The GSTN system, in this case, picks the FOB value as per the shipping bill. Thus, the refund amount would always be reduced proportionately to the value of insurance and freight expenses.

This would result in a loss of refund amount pertaining to the value of insurance and freight. This loss would be significant in cases where the cost of packing and transporting comprises a considerable proportion of value. The formula for the calculation of refund of ITC should be rationalised, and in the case of CIF contracts, the CIF value of the goods should be considered for the calculation of refund.

70. One single central GST account at the national level for companies having multi-state operations

In the current GST framework, businesses need to maintain separate state-level balances for Central Goods and Services Tax ('CGST') and State Goods and Services Tax ('SGST'). This system requires businesses operating in multiple states to manage separate CGST balances, which is cumbersome and often leads to inefficient utilisation of credits and cash flows.

Advantages of National-Level CGST Balances:

Improved Credit Utilization: A national-level CGST balance would allow businesses to offset liabilities across states, leading to better utilisation of available credits and cash.

Reduced Compliance Costs: Consolidating CGST balances reduces the complexity of financial management, making compliance easier and less expensive for businesses.

Enhanced Business Efficiency: National-level CGST balances would streamline tax management, allowing businesses to focus on core activities rather than managing disparate tax credits.

Benefits for the Government:

Reduced Operational Costs: The government would save on operational costs associated with managing multiple state-level CGST balances and streamline credit management.

Improved Revenue Management: A centralised system would give the government better oversight of national-level CGST credits, enabling more accurate revenue projections and collections.

Simplified Tax Administration: Centralizing CGST balances would simplify tax administration, allowing the government to reduce administrative complexities and improve efficiency.

71. Introduction of a centralised Appellate Authority for GST Advance Rulings

The proposal to establish a centralised Appellate Authority for Advance Rulings ('AAAR') was suggested by the 31st GST Council meeting to resolve cases where differing or conflicting decisions are made by Advance Ruling Authorities ('ARAs') in various states. Fast-tracking the implementation of this centralised authority is crucial for several reasons:

Current Challenges with State-Level ARAs:

Inconsistent Rulings: Different ARAs often issue contradictory rulings on the same issue, leading to uncertainty and confusion for businesses.

Increased Litigation: Conflicting rulings push businesses to challenge decisions, resulting in increased litigation and higher costs for both businesses and the government.

Operational Delays: Businesses face operational delays while seeking clarity on tax positions due to varying interpretations across states.

Benefits of a Centralized AAAR:

Uniformity in Rulings: A centralised AAAR would ensure consistency in rulings, providing businesses with a clear understanding of tax implications nationwide.

These questions guide the auditor towards understanding the business context behind the observed GST data patterns. This contextual understanding is paramount for correctly interpreting the data and distinguishing between legitimate business variations and potential compliance issues or irregularities.

Fundamental Analytical Procedures using GST Data (Ratio, Trend, Reconciliation)

There are several analytical procedures that auditors can perform using GST data:

Ratio Analysis:

-

GST payment to revenue ratio: Comparing this year-on-year can highlight changes in tax efficiency or business model.

-

Effective GST rate on sales vs. industry benchmarks: A significantly lower rate might indicate unreported exempt supplies, misclassification of goods/services, or even sales suppression.

-

Input tax credit (ITC) utilization rate over time: Fluctuations can point to changes in procurement patterns, capital asset purchases, or eligibility issues.

-

Output tax to sales ratio consistency analysis: Inconsistencies may signal errors in tax calculation or reporting.

-

Profitability ratio vs. GST Tax Payment (through banking channel) ratio: As discussed, a mismatch here is a key area for investigation.

Trend Analysis:

-

Quarter-on-quarter GST payment fluctuations vs. seasonal business patterns: Helps differentiate normal business cycles from anomalous payment behaviour.

-

Correlation between GST payments and declared profits: Analysing this trend over multiple periods can reveal emerging disconnects.

-

Trends in ITC utilization: Sudden spikes in ITC should be investigated; they could indicate large asset purchases, bulk raw material procurement, or erroneous claims. For example, if the monthly average GST ITC suddenly increases in a particular month, auditors should inquire about the reasons.

-

GST Credit Movement vs. Inventory Movement: Higher ITC accumulation at year-end might suggest significant inventory purchases towards the close of the financial year. Conversely, unutilized ITC can also be an indicator for assessing slow-moving or potentially obsolete inventory.

-

Impact of GST payments and refunds on cash flow management: Evaluating this helps understand the liquidity impact of GST on the entity.

Reconciliation Reviews:

-

GST turnover vs. financial statement turnover: This is a primary reconciliation to ensure completeness and accuracy of reported revenue.

-

E-way bill data vs. reported outward supplies: Comparing the volume and value of goods moved as per E-Way Bills with declared outward supplies in GSTR-1 can identify discrepancies.

-

Timing differences in revenue recognition criteria vs. GST time of supply: This is particularly crucial for export of goods, where revenue recognition in books might differ from the time of supply rules under GST, impacting reported turnover in a given period.

-

Input tax credits vs. major vendor payment patterns: Reconciling ITC claimed with payments made to major vendors can help identify potential fictitious ITC claims or non-payment to suppliers.

A consistent pattern of GST payments that are significantly lower than industry benchmarks, especially when coupled with high profitability, may warrant further examination to assess whether business model differences, tax position, cost structures, or reporting anomalies explain the observed deviation. or the availment of excessive, possibly ineligible, ITC. Such scenarios would warrant deeper scrutiny by the auditor.

Specified criteria

3. The scope of audits of bank branches is determined by these unique features of bank branches. Keeping in mind these nine unique features of bank branches, the auditors have to look into six specified things. These are :

(a ) Whether the liabilities and assets of the branch are correctly recorded in the Books of the Branch?

(b ) Whether these books and records are being maintained in accordance with instructions received from head office?

(c ) Whether assets shown in the books physically exist and are in satisfactory condition?

(d ) Whether the documents obtained by the Branch from its borrowers are complete in all respects and are legally enforceable?

(e ) Whether sanction letters for advance are properly kept and the instructions contained in such sanction letters are followed?

(f ) Whether proper and adequate returns are timely filed with Head Office?

Of Production or manufacture of goods;

Of stock of goods;

Period of maintenance of books of account

5. We are discussing about the maintenance of books of account and it is very important to know that for how much time we are required to preserve/retain the accounts. GST law provides that in normal situation a registered taxable person is required to retain such accounts and records till sixty months (60 Months/5 years) from the due date of filing of annual return for the year pertaining to such accounts and records.

However, in case the taxable person is a party to an appeal or revision, then accounts and records shall be retained for a period of one year (1 year) after final disposal of such appeal or revision or period discussed above, whichever is later.

6. Unlike Income-tax Act, the GST law also laid down the provisions with respect to audit of accounts maintained under this Act. This threshold limit shall be determined on PAN India basis.

This means that a person whose turnover during the financial year (FY) is more than INR 1 Crore shall be required to get its accounts audited. This will be required for each place of business. That means if a person having 4 branches in 4 different States, he must be having 4 separate registrations and the aggregate turnover of person is more than INR 1 Crore, then he shall be required to get the accounts audited for each separate registered States.

3.4 Customer-induced controls Currently, card-based payment systems provide customers with a ‘switch on/off’ facility for domestic and international use, as well as the ability to set limits for different transaction types. This facility has proven effective in empowering customers by enhancing their control over payment instruments and reducing fraud. However, similar user-controlled mechanisms are not uniformly available across other digital payment channels.

Accordingly, the RBI has proposed that customers can be provided with digital payment controls, including a ‘switch on/off’ facility for any digital payment mode, as well as the ability to set limits for different transaction types at the account level.

This would enable customers to control debit transactions at the account level across all or selected digital payment channels. Such facilities may be made accessible to the customer through bank branch visits, Internet banking, mobile banking, phone banking, Interactive Voice Response, or any other authenticated bank interfaces.

Further, it is proposed to introduce a single facility to disable all digital payment transactions from the account (‘kill switch’) at one stroke. Activation of the kill switch at the account level must override any other controls or configurations set up by the account holder.

Once the kill-switch is enabled, the account holder can reactivate digital payments either through digital channels, subject to proper authentication/verification, or by visiting a bank branch. To disable the kill switch via digital modes, banks may implement stringent authentication or verification measures to ensure proper customer identification.

Certain types of transactions, such as payment mandates and standing instructions, may be exempted from these controls and the kill switch.

In fraud situations, time is critical. A kill switch enables customers to immediately disable all digital payment access without having to navigate multiple systems or contact different banks.

The proposed framework aims to strengthen customer control over digital payment transactions by introducing account-level controls, including a unified ‘kill switch’. It enhances fraud prevention by enabling immediate disabling of digital payment access across channels. By extending such controls beyond card-based systems, it promotes uniform customer protection across all digital payment modes. Overall, it seeks to improve security, responsiveness, and customer confidence in digital banking.

4. Conclusion

What this paper really brings out is a simple shift in thinking. Digital payment fraud today is not happening because systems are weak, but because people are being misled. And once that happens, even the best systems can’t do much.

That’s where these proposals fit in. They don’t try to make payments more complex. Instead, they try to slow things down just enough, add a second layer of judgement where needed, and give users a bit more control when something feels off.

From a practical standpoint, this is important. Most users don’t think about fraud until it happens to them. Having built-in safeguards like a short delay, a trusted check, or even a kill switch can make a real difference in that one critical moment.

At the same time, the success of these measures will depend on how they are implemented. If they feel intuitive and not intrusive, users will accept them. If not, they risk being bypassed or ignored.

In a way, this is less about regulation and more about behaviour. The RBI is trying to redesign small parts of the payment journey so that people get a second to pause, think, and avoid a mistake they can’t easily undo. And if that works, it could quietly prevent a large number of frauds without most users even noticing it.

1. Demonetization has encouraged people to shift towards digital mode of payment while making financial transactions. By adopting digital mode of payment, no financial transactions would remain undisclosed and Consequently, an enhanced turnover of business might get reflected in the books of account.

Under the circumstances, an apprehension has been caused that increased turnover in the current year may lead to reopening of earlier years' cases causing undue harassment to taxpayers.

Thus, CBDT and CBEC (vide Circular No. 40/2016 and Circular No. 137/155/2012-Service tax) have advised tax officials not to re-open past assessments in income-tax and indirect tax cases only because increased turnover is reflected in books of account of business on account of increased use of digital means of payment.

2. Points to be considered for interpreting such circulars:

It would be incorrect to construe the above Circulars as giving any amnesty to tax-evaders.

The above circulars do not say that any spurt in turnover reported in books of account of businesses of current financial year (and consequently in their ITRs or indirect tax returns) is not need to be explained.

The Circulars do not give businessmen a license to show their accumulated black money in the form of demonetized notes as current year's turnover and get away scot-free without any interest or penalty and by paying normal tax for current year. If such a license is given by the circulars, the proposed PMGKY Scheme and proposed amendments to section115BBE of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and proposed new section 271AAC of that Act would be redundant.

The two circulars clarify the following points which is mere re-iteration of the existing law:

Suppose any business reported Rs.1cr to Rs.1.5 cr as its turnover in service tax and VAT in last 5 years. If the business reports a turnover of Rs.5 cr in financial year 2016-17, then it is natural for any tax official to suspect that increased turnover;

However, such suspicion alone is not sufficient to entail reopening of past assessments in income-tax and well as service tax/customs;

The Circulars do not take away the powers of tax officials to make inquiries into the sudden spurt in reported turnover;

If the results of enquiries yield information which can form basis of "reason to believe" escapement of turnover/income in the past periods, the assessments can be reopened.

The Circulars are innocuous and merely caution tax officials to adopt systematic approach under the law to enquire into sudden jumps and reopen past assessment only if enquiry throws up reason to believe that past turnovers/incomes escaped assessment. Sudden jump in turnover may give reason to suspect that turnover/income had escaped assessment in past years. But that suspicion should not lead to reopening of past assessments without making necessary inquiries and verification regarding causes of the sudden increase.

Huge increase in reported turnover can be due to genuine reasons as well as due to book-keeping sophistry.

53. Allowing utilisation of the input tax credit ledger balance for reverse charge payments

Under the GST law, certain provisions result in cash blockages without yielding any incremental revenue to the Government. For instance, in the case of imports of services, the recipient of services is liable to discharge GST liability in cash under a reverse charge mechanism, which will then be available to him as ITC. The mandatory cash payment leads to cash blockage.

The Government should consider allowing taxpayers to use their GST ITC balance for payment of tax under the reverse charge mechanism. The ability to use the ITC balance to discharge the RCM liability would not only address the cash flow issues but also streamline the tax administration process, making it more business-friendly without compromising the tax revenues for the Government.

54. Transfer of Input Tax Credit from one State to another

Under the existing GST framework, Form ITC-02 facilitates the transfer of unutilised input tax credit only between GST registrations located within the same State. The law does not currently envisage or provide any mechanism for transferring accumulated ITC in cases of inter-State business movement. Consequently, in situations such as business reorganisation, merger or restructuring involving different States, closure of operations or a branch in one State, and continuation of the same business from another State, the accumulated ITC remains locked with the original registration. This results in a loss of credit, a blockage of working capital, and procedural hardship, despite no change in the underlying business or tax incidence.

Recently, the Bombay High Court in the case of Umicore Autocat India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2025) 32 Centax 416 (Bom.), pursuant to a scheme of amalgamation, held that the transfer of unutilized ITC lying in the electronic credit ledger of transferor company to amalgamated company is allowed irrespective of fact that companies are located in different States.

It is recommended that a procedure be devised to allow for the transfer of accumulated ITC in such inter-state business transfers, to ensure seamless credit flow and avoid loss of legitimate credits to taxpayers.

55. Refund of the closing balance of the Input Tax Credit

Under the erstwhile VAT regime, taxpayers were permitted to claim a refund of unutilized input tax credit (ITC) at the end of the financial year. This ensured that taxes already paid on inputs did not become a permanent cost to businesses and supported adequate working capital management.

Under the GST framework, the refund of accumulated ITC is currently available only in limited circumstances, such as for zero-rated supplies (exports and supplies to SEZs) and for inverted duty structures. In most other situations, unutilized ITC remains blocked, even though it represents taxes already paid to the Government.

A critical situation arises when a taxpayer decides to close or exit a business. Currently, the GST law does not explicitly provide for the refund of unutilized ITC upon business closure, leaving taxpayers unable to recover legitimate credits accumulated over the course of operations. This creates an unnecessary financial burden, as the unutilized credit represents tax that has already been paid and should rightfully be refundable.

It is therefore recommended that a provision be introduced under GST allowing:

Refund of unutilized ITC at the end of a financial year, to ease working capital constraints.

Refund of accumulated ITC on business closure, enabling taxpayers to recover input taxes legitimately paid, thereby reducing stranded credit and avoiding penalisation of businesses for exiting operations.

Introduced in the Union Budget of 2019, the Legacy Dispute Resolution Scheme was designed to clear the backlog of disputes under various central indirect tax laws. 73. Allowing small-scale ice cream manufacturers to opt for a composition scheme

The GST law allows certain taxpayers with turnover up to Rs. 1.5 Crores to opt for a composition scheme, which enables them to pay GST at lower rates and comply with fewer compliance requirements. However, this scheme is not available to all taxpayers as the law provides a specific restriction for a list of persons who cannot opt to pay tax under the composition scheme. This list includes manufacturers of Pan Masala, Tobacco, Ice Cream, and other edible items. This restriction was introduced based on the recommendation of the 17th GST Council meeting.

Small-scale ice cream manufacturers have criticised this restriction, arguing that ice cream has been placed on par with Pan Masala and Tobacco without adequate justification. They contend that ice cream is a widely consumed item and should not be arbitrarily classified as a luxury good without proper reasoning.

Recently, this issue came before the Chhattisgarh High Court, wherein the Hon'ble Court directed31 the GST Council to reconsider the exclusion of small-scale ice cream manufacturers from the composition scheme. The Court highlighted that the GST Council had provided no specific reason to exclude Ice Cream Manufacturers from the benefit of the composition scheme, and it should have considered the socio-economic impact of placing ice cream in the 18% tax rate. A similar order was earlier passed by Delhi High Court32 on the same matter.

The issue is expected to be covered in the upcoming budget.

FAQ 25. What documents should be maintained by the taxpayers to comply with the requirement of maintenance of books of accounts as per section 44AA?

The following documents should be maintained by the taxpayers to comply with the requirement of maintenance of books of accounts : FAQ 26. Mr A is maintaining books of accounts at more than one location. Whether the address of all the locations is to be mentioned in the audit report?

Clause 11 of Form 3CD requires a list of books maintained and the address where such books of accounts are kept. If such books of accounts are kept at multiple locations, the auditor must mention the address of all the locations and the details of books of accounts maintained at each location. In the case of a company assessee, the auditor should verify whether Form AOC-5 has been filed with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act for maintenance of books of accounts at a place other than the registered office.

The auditor's duties regarding 'books of account maintained' are not limited to merely giving a list of books of account against clause 11(b). He is required to examine the books of account maintained. Based on such examination, he is required to state in Form No. 3CB, whether books of account kept are 'proper books of account'.

FAQ 27. An assessee has changed the method of accounting from mercantile to cash basis. What disclosure is required in Form 3CD?

Clause 13 of Form 3CD requires every assessee to report the method of accounting employed in the previous year. Further, if there was a change in the method employed in the immediately preceding previous year, then the same is to be reported. The assessee is also required to disclose the effect of a change in the method of accounting on the profit and loss. If it is not possible to quantify the effect of a change in the method of accounting, appropriate disclosure should be made under this clause.

A change in accounting policy will not amount to a change in the method of accounting, and hence any change in the accounting policies need not be mentioned under clause 13(b).

FAQ 28. Whether adoption of Ind AS for the first time could be considered as 'Change in Method of Accounting' for disclosure in Form 3CD?

Method of Accounting refers to the basic rules and guidelines under which businesses keep their financial records and prepare their financial statements. There are two main accounting methods used for record-keeping - the Cash Basis and the Accrual Basis. Whereas the Accounting Standards or Ind AS pre-requisite the accrual basis of accounting. Accounting standards are authoritative standards for financial reporting and are the primary source of generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP).

Method of Accounting should not be confused with GAAP. Method of Accounting can be either a cash basis or accrual basis. The GAAP provides the principles and procedures for calculation and recognition of a financial transaction within the framework of Accrual basis of accounting. When an entity switches from Accounting Standards to Ind AS, it does not change its method of accounting. Thus, the transition to Ind AS should not be treated as a change in the method of accounting.

FAQ 29. Whether GST registration no. of the assessee has to be furnished in Form 3CD if the assessee is liable to pay tax under reverse charge?

The ICAI, vide Implementation Guide dated August 22, 2018, has clarified that even if liability to pay GST is only under the reverse charge mechanism, the fact of being liable to GST needs to be answered in the affirmative, with the clarification that such liability is only under the reverse charge mechanism.

FAQ 30. If an assessee has multiple GSTIN, which registration no. must be furnished in Form 3CD?

If the assessee has multiple GSTIN numbers (registered in different states), all the GSTIN numbers allotted to him shall be mentioned in Form 3CD.

Total payment to registered entities.
