12.6-2d From the account(s) maintained by the recipient with the banker

(i) Generally, account and types

What is the meaning of "account"? It means a recipient's (ledger) account with the bank in/from which deposits/withdrawals are made and accounted.

The account(s) must be maintained by the recipient. Possibly, it implies that the recipient is the beneficial and the legal owner of the account(s), jointly or severally, and operates accordingly.

Any person can have a bank account in his own name; he may have more than one bank accounts; he may be having joint accounts with family members or others; he may be only a signatory in a bank account; the account of partnership or association of persons or a trust may be in the name of a person and so on.

In such a case, to ascertain the withdrawal in cash and that too beyond the threshold limit, which account or accounts need to be considered and can there be any aggregation?

(ii) Account held for Entities

Suppose, an individual is acting in the designated capacity for and on behalf of either a trust or any other entity, can it be said that the account is maintained by the recipient, that is, the individual? In such a case, it cannot be said that merely because an individual is a title holder or a signatory in a bank account for and on behalf of an entity, the account is maintained by him. In fact, the account maintained is of the trust or other entity.

(iii) Joint - Account

Suppose, an individual is a joint holder of a bank account along with his family members and others; such an account is also operated by the individual. The joint holding could be on account of various reasons and an individual may not necessarily have the beneficial ownership. Can such account be considered as maintained by all the joint holders jointly or severally? If it is joint, is it a separate account from the one maintained by the recipient? If it is considered as several, whether the transactions in such a joint account can be considered in the hands of all the joint holders? Mode and manner of dealing with such an account are not very clear from the provision and would pose several difficulties both to the banker as well as the recipients.

Would it be possible for a bank to take a view that in case of joint holding, the first name holder would be considered as the person withdrawing cash for the purposes of the section?

If there is joint ownership, another challenge would be in whose name TDS would be made and who would get credit for the same?

In the light of the above, the position may have to be determined having regard to the terms of contract, information relating to the same and clarifications which may be issued by the authorities from time to time in that behalf.

Depending on the treatment given by the banker in respect of the accounts held singly or jointly by any person, the person may have tax deduction from such bank account (whether belonging to him or otherwise) as well as additional information in respect of him furnished by the banker to tax department; if the person concerned has not reported, say, a bank account jointly held with another person and the other person has reported such bank account in his return, the first person will need to explain why the jointly held bank account was not reported and about debits and credits in such account.

Another issue which may have to be resolved is the manner of applying the threshold limit in case of joint banking account.

(iv) One or more accounts

A recipient has bank accounts in its own name with various branches of the bank; in such a case, it would be necessary to aggregate the transactions in all the bank accounts and accordingly discharge the obligations. The cash transactions in all the accounts, as they are with a single banking company, will have to be aggregated to enable the bank to discharge its obligations. Which branch should do it, may be the prerogative of the bank or can it be said that the bank branch from which the withdrawal is effected would be responsible for deducting tax?

A person may have different types of banking account, like, saving account, current account, fixed deposit account, recurring deposit account and so on. Suppose, all the accounts are in the name of single individual. Prima facie, to ascertain the applicability of the provisions, the transactions in all the accounts may have to be aggregated.

(v) Foreign branch

Suppose, a resident recipient has an account with a foreign branch of any Indian bank and effects withdrawal from (in foreign currency) such a bank account, the moot question is whether the bank is obliged to apply the provision to such account?

(i) Generally, account and types

What is the meaning of "account"? It means a recipient's (ledger) account with the bank in/from which deposits/withdrawals are made and accounted.

The account(s) must be maintained by the recipient. Possibly, it implies that the recipient is the beneficial and the legal owner of the account(s), jointly or severally, and operates accordingly.

Any person can have a bank account in his own name; he may have more than one bank accounts; he may be having joint accounts with family members or others; he may be only a signatory in a bank account; the account of partnership or association of persons or a trust may be in the name of a person and so on.

In such a case, to ascertain the withdrawal in cash and that too beyond the threshold limit, which account or accounts need to be considered and can there be any aggregation?

(ii) Account held for Entities

Suppose, an individual is acting in the designated capacity for and on behalf of either a trust or any other entity, can it be said that the account is maintained by the recipient, that is, the individual? In such a case, it cannot be said that merely because an individual is a title holder or a signatory in a bank account for and on behalf of an entity, the account is maintained by him. In fact, the account maintained is of the trust or other entity.

(iii) Joint - Account

Suppose, an individual is a joint holder of a bank account along with his family members and others; such an account is also operated by the individual. The joint holding could be on account of various reasons and an individual may not necessarily have the beneficial ownership. If it is considered as several, whether the transactions in such a joint account can be considered in the hands of all the joint holders? Mode and manner of dealing with such an account are not very clear from the provision and would pose several difficulties both to the banker as well as the recipients.

12.6-2e Deduction from payment in excess of the threshold - Deduction of tax is required, by the banker, only after the payment exceeds the threshold specified of Rs. 1 crore; till payment in cash of Rs. 1 crore, there is no obligation (For detailed discussion, see para 12.6-3); if the payment in cash exceeds Rs. 1 crore, tax needs to be deducted only from the payments in excess of the threshold (and not the entire amount including Rs. 1 crore); to illustrate, a person has withdrawn Rs. 99 lakhs and proposes to withdraw Rs. 5 lakhs; the excess over the threshold is Rs. 4 lakhs; accordingly the banker is required to deduct tax at 2% from Rs. 4 lakhs of Rs. 8000.

Apparently, such deduction would be reflected in the bank account as deduction of tax.

The threshold limit would apply in respect of each previous year separately; if the withdrawal in cash, say, in previous year 1 is in excess of the threshold limit, on the excess, the bank would be required to deduct tax; however, if, in previous year 2, the cash withdrawal does not exceed the threshold limit, no tax can be deducted.

12.6-2f Credit for tax deducted - Having regard to the provisions relating to the credit, it may be said that the credit may not be available on the ground that the provision granting credit, namely, section 199, allows credit of tax deducted from income; as discussed above, the deduction cannot be considered as one from income paid to the recipient.

However, such literal reading may not be adopted and the recipient should be able to claim credit thereof as payment of tax in advance or other payment of taxes, having regard to the fact that it is not a separate or independent levy and it represents a mere collection of tax through the mechanism of deduction by the banker which may or may not be strictly construed as deduction of tax at source as is understood having regard to the provisions of Chapter XVII-B.

In addition to the above, having regard to the information required to be furnished by the banker, possibly, the recipient may also end up explaining to the tax authorities that the withdrawals do not represent any separate independent income and that they represent withdrawal of his own money from and out of his income or other cash flows.

There may also be difficulty about who is eligible for credit of tax deducted out of the withdrawals from a joint bank account.

(1) Whether Conversion Charges paid in cash to as payee's bank account was frozen by attachment order of ESIC?

Where the assessee-company had paid conversion charges to a company in cash as a bank account of the said company was frozen by an order of attachment passed by the ESI department, the assessee was entitled to exemption under rule 6DD and; thus, no disallowance under section 40A(3) was called for. What is crucial while testing such a

GENERAL

Constitutional validity - Section 281B gives guidelines for making provisional attachment and is, thus, constitutionally valid [Dar International v. Asstt. DIT [1995] 82 Taxman 75 (Delhi)].

Search proceedings - Such proceedings which are to be necessarily commenced as a result of search are to be treated as 'proceedings' within meaning of section 281B(1). Therefore, an order passed u/s 281B could not be questioned on ground that no assessment proceedings were pending on date of passing of such order [Nimitya Properties Ltd. v. CIT [2010] 194 Taxman 135 (Delhi)].

SARFAESI Act - In the absence of any specific provision under the Securitisation Act creating first charge on bank, section 281B r/w Rule 16 of Second Schedule will have an overriding effect on section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act [UCO Bank-Regional Office v. UOI [2009] 182 Taxman 26 (Guj.)].

PROPERTY

Membership card - Membership card of a member of Ahmedabad Stock Exchange, who had been declared as a deemed defaulter and whose right vested in stock exchange, could not be said to be property of that assessee so as to be attached u/s 281B [Stock Exchange v. Asstt. CIT [2001] 115 Taxman 471 (SC)].

Letters of credit (LC) - Letters of credit (LCs) issued by Indian bank on behalf of a resident party dealing with a foreign party to secure payment of dues from resident are assets which can be provisionally attached u/s 281B during pendency of proceedings to protect interests of revenue in respect of tax payable by foreign party in respect of amount receivable under those LCs [Royal Bank of Scotland PLC v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2017] 85 taxmann.com 73/250 Taxman 392 (SC)].

ATTACHMENT

Exercise of power - Power of attachment of property u/s 281B should be exercised by the AO only if there is reasonable apprehension that assessee is about to dispose of whole or any part of his property with a view to thwart ultimate collection of demand [Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 (Bom.)].

The power conferred upon the AO u/s 281B is a very drastic far-reaching power and that power has to be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and reasons. To ensure that this power is not misused, a number of safeguards have been provided in the section itself. One thing is clear that this power should be exercised by the AO only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and caution. It should not be exercised unless there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of the demand [Society for Integrated Development in Urban and Rural Areas v. CIT [2001] 119 Taxman 289 (AP)].

Assessee cannot compel which property to be attached - As to which of the assets could have been attached, it is the subjective satisfaction of the assessing authority. It is for him to decide as to which of the assets could be liquidated without difficulty for realisation of the tax assessed. The assessee cannot compel the AO to attach any particular property [VLS Finance Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 112 Taxman 295 (Delhi)].

Attachment of assessee's property only - Attachment order was to be limited to plot owner by person against whom order was passed and not extended to plots owned by others in residential area [Mutta Venkata Ramana v. ITO [2013] 40 taxmann.com 531/[2014] 221 Taxman 222 (Mag.) (AP); Raghunandan Enterprise v. Asstt. CIT [2022] 139 taxmann.com 51 (Guj.)].

Attachment of bank accounts and trading assets - Attachment should be made as far as possible of immovable properties if that can protect Revenue, therefore, attachment of bank accounts and trading assets should be resorted to only as a last resort [Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 (Bom.); Society for Integrated Development in Urban and Rural Areas v. CIT [2001] 119 Taxman 289 (AP)].

6.10

PROCEEDS OF BENAMI PROPERTY DEPOSITED IN BANK

Cash and bank balance are treated as movable property/asset. Property under section 2(26) of PBPT Act, 1988 means asset of any kind, whether movable or immovable and proceeds of a such property. It is our common knowledge that on many occasions cash forms part of the proceeds of a benami property which gets deposited in bank. In such a situation, depending on the origin of cash and intention behind such a transaction, the balance in the bank account represented by proceeds of a benami property could form benami property. In other words, if the bank balance has a nexus with the proceeds of a benami property, it can partake the character of benami property subject to benami transaction. There may a case where there is no bank balance except leaving a very small balance and there is no trace of utilization of cash withdrawn. Action can be taken to attach the small amount of cash balance in the bank and then other consequences would follow. There is no monetary limit to initiate benami proceeding.

The nature of Personal Deposit Account is explained by the High Court in Kurumber Betta Estate v. ITO [2002] 257 ITR 328/124 Taxman 161 (Ker.) as follows:

"We are informed that under administrative circulars, amounts which were not to be appropriated to the revenue are held in personal deposit account to be kept in the name of certain officers, including TRO. These amounts are actually treated as amounts of the Government over which the bank has no authority. In other words, instead of depositing the amount in the treasury, the bank holds it as an agent of the treasury for the purpose of holding the money. Such amounts which are held as security cannot be utilised by the bank, would not bear any interest, and the revenue also would not be entitled to any interest on such amount held. All amounts which are collected otherwise than by way of tax or penalty are credited to this personal deposit account. Amounts such as seized cash are also credited to this account."

This amendment, removing the precondition for the AO to form an opinion, has effectively expanded the AO's authority to withhold refunds. The AO now has the authority to withhold refunds after recording the reasons, even if the reasons given do not adversely affect revenue. There are numerous rulings in which the courts have ruled in favour of the assessee where the facts of the case did not justify the claim of AO that granting the refund would adversely affect revenue. Here are a few examples of refund withholdings that were overturned due to the failure to meet the condition that "granting the refund is likely to adversely affect the revenue."

(a)

In this case, the assessee deducted and deposited TDS on payment under the old TAN as well as the new TAN due to human error, which resulted in the TDS mismatch. The computer system could not rectify the error or duplicate entries. The Bombay High Court held that the department could not withhold the refund payable to the assessee merely because it could not rectify the duplication of entry in the old TAN and new TAN, resulting in the TDS mismatch [Vodafone Idea Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2019] 106 taxmann.com 22 (Bom.)].

(b)

In this case, the Bombay High Court held that where the assessee filed its return declaring loss and claimed refund of the entire amount of tax paid at source, merely because in the immediately preceding assessment year, the assessee had declared a positive income as against substantial loss declared in the relevant assessment year, it could not be a ground to doubt contents of return or claim of the assessee with respect to loss suffered and withhold refund claimed by the assessee [Vodafone Idea Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2019] 111 taxmann.com 451/267 Taxman 603 (Bom.)].

(c)

In this case, the Supreme Court held that the AO withheld the refund based on an estimation that the petitioner might incur a substantial tax liability concerning unearned revenue and advances. This is not justified. The petitioner consistently followed an accounting policy of recognising unearned revenue in its books and offering it for tax as services were rendered [Ericsson India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2022] 136 taxmann.com 228 (Del.)].

(d)

The Bombay High Court held that there is no power vested in revenue authorities to adjust admitted refunds against tax dues, which are not even adjudicated upon by tax authorities and may arise in future. Where revenue authorities had already invoked their powers under section 245, and an order was passed, they could not withhold the admitted refundable amount on the ground that respondents might have a future demand against the assessee arising out of pending assessment orders [Vodafone Idea Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2020] 117 taxmann.com 597 (Bom.)].

In all the cases mentioned above, the courts have overturned the withholding of demands, as the facts did not justify the claim of the AO that granting the refund would likely have an adverse effect on the revenue. With the removal of this pre-condition, all these cases would fall within the scope of the AO's power to withhold refunds by merely recording the reasons.

The power to withhold refunds is not absolute and must be exercised judiciously, balancing taxpayers' rights with the need to safeguard revenue interests. The AO must record the reasoned order before withholding the refund, which is an essential principle of natural justice. The Apex Court in the case of Kranti Associates (P.) Ltd. v. Masood Ahmed Khan [2010] 9 SCC 496 has discussed the importance of passing a speaking order and observed "the need to give reasons in support of the decision/order, in all proceedings (whether administrative or quasi-judicial) which affect the rights of the parties involved. From time to time, the court has held that the face of an order passed by a quasi-judicial authority or even an administrative authority affecting the parties' rights must speak. It must not be like the 'inscrutable face of Sphinx'."

The AO3 should consider the following factors while exercising powers to withhold a refund and should pass a speaking order justifying the refund withholding:

Prima facie view on the grounds for the issuance of notice under section 143(2);

The amount of tax liability that the scrutiny assessment may eventually result in vis-a-vis the amount of tax refund due to the assessee.

The creditworthiness or financial standing of the assessee.

To safeguard the assessee against arbitrary order to withhold the refund, the CBDT has specified4 that provisions of Section 245(2) shall apply only when the refund amount is Rs. 10 lakhs or more. Therefore, the Assessing Officer cannot withhold refunds less than Rs. 10 lakhs.

As per the instruction, in cases where section 245(2) is applicable, the Faceless Assessing Officer (FAO), upon receiving communication from the Centralised Processing Centre (CPC), must inform the Jurisdictional AO about the potential demand in the pending assessment(s). The Jurisdictional AO, upon receiving information from the FAO, shall document the reasons in writing with due diligence and analysis of the case's factual context, which includes:

(a)

The financial condition of the taxpayer.

(b)

Past demands.

2.8-2 Would the provisions of maintenance of books of accounts under section 44AA apply? All presumptive schemes, except under sections 44BBC and 44BBD, allow the assessee to rebut the presumptive income and compute the income after maintaining the books of account under section 44AA and get them audited under section 44AB. In the absence of any relaxation given to the assessee opting for sections 44BBC and 44BBD presumptive schemes, it seems that the maintenance of the books of account may be a mandatory requirement for such assessees if the gross turnover or receipts exceed the threshold limit.

2.8-3 Would the provisions of tax audit under section 44AB apply?

Tax audits under section 44AB serve no useful purpose when the assessment is made on a presumptive basis. They serve a useful purpose for the Income Tax Department only when the assessee's income is computed under the regular provisions based on the books of account maintained by the assessee, and allowances and disallowances are to be made according to the requirements of sections 28 to 43A. This is clear from CBDT's Circular No. 387, dated 6-7-1984, which explains the rationale for the introduction of section 44AB as follows:

"17.1 Compulsory audit of accounts of certain persons carrying on business or profession - Accounts maintained by companies are re-quired to be audited under the Companies Act, 1956. Accounts maintained by co-operative societies are also required to be audited under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912. There is, however, no obligation on other categories of taxpayers to get their accounts audited.

17.2 A proper audit for tax purposes would ensure that the books of account and other records are properly maintained, that they faithfully re-flect the income of the taxpayer and claims for deduction are correctly made by him. Such audit would also help in checking fraudulent practices. It can also facilitate the administration of tax laws by a proper presentation of the accounts before the tax authorities and considerably saving the time of Assessing Officers in carrying out routine verifications, like checking correctness of totals and verifying whether purchases and sales are properly vouched or not. The time of the Assessing Officers thus saved could be utilised for attending to more important investigational aspects of a case."

That is the reason why provisions like sections 44ADA, 44AE and 44BBB exempt the assessee from tax audit under section 44AB when his income is liable to be computed on a presumptive basis under those sections and require tax audit only when the assessee opts out of those presumptive tax provisions. Regarding section 44BBC and section 44BBD, no consequential amendment has been made to the second proviso to section 44AB to exempt assessees covered by sections 44BBC and 44BBD from tax audit under section 44AB. Thus, it appears that in the absence of any relaxation given to the assessee opting for sections 44BBC and 44BBD presumptive schemes, it seems that the audit of the books of account may be a mandatory requirement for such assessees if the gross turnover or receipts exceed the threshold limit.

Applying section 44AA and section 44AB to an assessee opting for the presumptive scheme would defeat the core purpose of introducing section 44BBD, which aimed to eliminate the maintenance of books of account and simplify compliance for non-residents.

2.8-4 Will the GST collected from the resident company be part of the specified amount?

A question would arise whether GST collected from the resident company would form part of the specified amount for computing the presumptive profit of 25% of the said amount. There are judicial decisions50 in the context of similarly worded presumptive tax provisions of section 44B/section 44BB that service tax collected by the assessee and passed on to the Government does not have any element of income and, therefore, cannot form part of gross receipts for purposes of computing 'presumptive in-come'.

Given the above judicial decisions rendered in the context of sections 44B and 44BB, it appears that GST collected from the resident company would not form part of the specified amount for computing the presumptive profit of 25%.

2.8-2 Would the provisions of maintenance of books of accounts under section 44AA apply? All presumptive schemes, except under sections 44BBC and 44BBD, allow the assessee to rebut the presumptive income and compute the income after maintaining the books of account under section 44AA and get them audited under section 44AB. In the absence of any relaxation given to the assessee opting for sections 44BBC and 44BBD presumptive schemes, it seems that the maintenance of the books of account may be a mandatory requirement for such assessees if the gross turnover or receipts exceed the threshold limit.

2.8-3 Would the provisions of tax audit under section 44AB apply?

Tax audits under section 44AB serve no useful purpose when the assessment is made on a presumptive basis. They serve a useful purpose for the Income Tax Department only when the assessee's income is computed under the regular provisions based on the books of account maintained by the assessee, and allowances and disallowances are to be made according to the requirements of sections 28 to 43A. This is clear from CBDT's Circular No. 387, dated 6-7-1984, which explains the rationale for the introduction of section 44AB as follows:

"17.1 Compulsory audit of accounts of certain persons carrying on business or profession - Accounts maintained by companies are required to be audited under the Companies Act, 1956. Accounts maintained by co-operative societies are also required to be audited under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912. There is, however, no obligation on other categories of taxpayers to get their accounts audited.

17.2 A proper audit for tax purposes would ensure that the books of account and other records are properly maintained, that they faithfully reflect the income of the taxpayer and claims for deduction are correctly made by him. Such audit would also help in checking fraudulent practices. It can also facilitate the administration of tax laws by a proper presentation of the accounts before the tax authorities and considerably saving the time of Assessing Officers in carrying out routine verifications, like checking correctness of totals and verifying whether purchases and sales are properly vouched or not. The time of the Assessing Officers thus saved could be utilised for attending to more important investigational aspects of a case."

That is the reason why provisions like sections 44ADA, 44AE and 44BBB exempt the assessee from tax audit under section 44AB when his income is liable to be computed on a presumptive basis under those sections and require tax audit only when the assessee opts out of those presumptive tax provisions. Regarding section 44BBC and section 44BBD, no consequential amendment has been made to the second proviso to section 44AB to exempt assessees covered by sections 44BBC and 44BBD from tax audit under section 44AB. Thus, it appears that in the absence of any relaxation given to the assessee opting for sections 44BBC and 44BBD presumptive schemes, it seems that the audit of the books of account may be a mandatory requirement for such assessees if the gross turnover or receipts exceed the threshold limit.

Applying section 44AA and section 44AB to an assessee opting for the presumptive scheme would defeat the core purpose of introducing section 44BBD, which aimed to eliminate the maintenance of books of account and simplify compliance for non-residents.

2.8-4 Will the GST collected from the resident company be part of the specified amount?

A question would arise whether GST collected from the resident company would form part of the specified amount for computing the presumptive profit of 25% of the said amount. There are judicial decisions50 in the context of similarly worded presumptive tax provisions of section 44B/section 44BB that service tax collected by the assessee and passed on to the Government does not have any element of income and, therefore, cannot form part of gross receipts for purposes of computing 'presumptive income'.

Given the above judicial decisions rendered in the context of sections 44B and 44BB, it appears that GST collected from the resident company would not form part of the specified amount for computing the presumptive profit of 25%.

Search and seizure - Intrusion into privacy

Search and seizure is an "intrusion" into the privacy of a man. The earliest case to deal with the "privacy" and "search and seizure" was M. P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra [1954] SCR 1077 in the context of article 19(1)(f) and article 20(3) of the Constitution of India. The contention that search and seizure violated the article 19(1)(f) was rejected, the court holding that that a mere search by itself did not affect any right to property, and though seizure affected it, such effect was only temporary and was a reasonable restriction on the right. The question whether search warrants for the seizure of documents from the accused were unconstitutional was not gone into.

The right to privacy is not absolute. The intrusion must be based upon showing probable cause. Intrusion may be by —

(1) legislative provisions,

(2) administrative/executive orders and

(3) judicial orders.

The legislative intrusion must be tested on the touchstone of reasonableness as guaranteed by the Constitution and for that purpose the court can go into the proportionality of the intrusion vis-a-vis the purpose sought to be achieved. So far as administrative or executive action is concerned, it has again to be reasonable having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case. As to judicial warrants, the court must have sufficient reason to believe that the search and seizure is warranted and it must keep in mind the extent of search or seizure necessary for the protection of the particular state interest. In addition, common law recognized rare exceptions such as where warrantless search could be conducted but these must be in good faith, intended to preserve evidence or intended to prevent sudden danger to person or property.

In R. v. Jeffries (1994) (1) NZLR 290, Robertson J., stated that the reasonableness of a search and seizure would depend upon the subject- matter and the unique combination of "time, place and circumstances". The court made a distinction between illegality and reasonableness of the search or seizure, in the context of section 21 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights, 1990. It said, "a search may be legal but unreasonable; it may be illegal but reasonable". Probably, what was meant was that a search under a court warrant may be lawful but the manner in which it is executed may be unreasonable. Likewise, there may be very rare exceptions where a search and seizure operation is conducted without a warrant on account of a sense of grave urgency for preventing danger to life or property or where delay in procuring a warrant may indeed result in the evidence vanishing but still the search or seizure might have been conducted in a reasonable manner.

In the Income-tax Act, 1961, elaborate provisions are made in regard to "search and seizure" in section 132; power to requisition books of account, etc. in section 132A; power to call for information as stated in section 133. Section 133(6) deals with power of officers to require any bank to furnish any information as specified there. There safeguards. Section 132 uses the words "in consequence of information in his possession, has reason to believe". Section 132(1A) uses the words "in consequence of information in his possession, has reason to suspect." Section 132(13) says that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, relating to searches and seizure shall apply, so far as may be, to searches and seizure under section 132(1) and 132(1A). There are also rules made under section 132(14). Likewise section 132A(1) uses the words "in consequence of information in his possession, has reason to believe". Section 133 which deals with the power to call for information from banks and other uses the words "for the purpose of this Act" and section 133(6) permits requisition to be sent to the bank or its officer. There are other Central and State statutes dealing with procedure for ‘search and seizure’ for the purpose of the respective statutes.

Under all these enactments, the Supreme Court explained the scope of the provisions and the safeguards provided by those provisions while upholding the constitutional validity and pointing out the limitations. 43.11 Payment of refund amount through PFMS

The sanctioned refund amounts, as entered in the payment orders issued by the Central and State/UT tax officers, shall be disbursed through the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) of the Controller General of Accounts (CGA), Ministry of Finance, Government of India.

On filing of a refund application in FORM GST RFD-01, the common portal shall generate a master file for the applicant containing the relevant details like name, GSTIN, bank account details etc. This master file shall be shared with PFMS for validation of the bank account details provided by the applicant in the refund application. Once the bank account is validated, PFMS will create a unique assessee code (combination of GSTIN + validated bank account number) for the applicant. This unique assessee code will be used by PFMS for all refund payments made to the applicant in the said bank account.

In order to avoid repeat validations and generation of multiple unique assessee codes for the same GSTIN, it shall be advisable for the applicants to enter the same bank account details in successive refund applications submitted in FORM GST RFD-01. In cases where an applicant wishes to avail the refund in a different bank account, which has not yet been validated, a new unique assessee code (comprising of GSTIN + new bank account) will be generated by PFMS after validation of the said bank account - para 28 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019 - GST dated 18-11-2019.

43.11-1 If bank account details mentioned are invalidated

If the bank account details mentioned by an applicant in the refund application submitted in FORM GST RFD-01 are invalidated, an error message shall be transmitted by PFMS to the common portal electronically and the common portal shall make the error message available to the applicant and the refund officers on their dashboards. On receiving such an error message, an applicant can - (a) rectify the invalidated bank account details by filing a non-core amendment in FORM GST REG-14; or (b) add a new bank account by filing a non-core amendment in FORM GST REG-14 - para 29 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019 - GST dated 18-11-2019.

The updated bank account details will be reflected in a drop-down menu on the dashboard. From this drop-down menu, the applicant can choose any bank account, including the ones rectified (option (a)) or newly added (option (b)), from the list of bank accounts available in his registration database. The chosen bank account details will again be sent to PFMS for validation. The proper officer will be able to issue the payment order in FORM GST RFD-05 only after the selected bank account has been validated - para 30 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019 - GST dated 18-11-2019.

By following the above process, validation errors, if any, will generally be corrected before the issuance of payment order in FORM GST RFD-05. Therefore, there should generally not be any validation errors after issuance of a payment order in FORM GST RFD-05. However, in certain exceptional cases, it is possible that a validation error occurs after issuance of the payment order. In such cases, the said payment order will be invalidated by the common portal and a new payment order will have to be issued by the proper officer after following the rectification process described in paras 29 and 30 above.

The re-issued payment order will have a new reference number and shall contain the newly selected bank account details. However, there will be no change in either the original ARN or the sanction order number or the amount for which the payment order was originally issued - para 31 of CBI&C Circular No. 125/44/2019 - GST dated 18-11-2019.

Since, the withdrawals are from two different accounts, it may not attract BCTT.

Situation 2 :

Suppose an individual issued a bearer cheque to another person for Rs. 15,000, say, on June 5, 2005 drawn on bank account No. 12345. On June 7, he withdraws cash of Rs. 12,000 from the said account in the morning and another person encashes the cheque on June 7, 2005. Both the withdrawals, in aggregate, exceed Rs. 25,000 in a single day and accordingly, would be liable to BCTT.

Situation 3 :

Suppose, an individual has two accounts, in different branches, of the same scheduled bank, in the same town or different towns. He withdraws Rs. 16,000 from one account and Rs. 15,000 from another account. The aggregate withdrawals are Rs. 31,000.

Apparently, both the withdrawals may not be considered as taxable banking transactions attracting BCTT, since the withdrawal must be from ‘an’ account which implies one account, as explained above.

Situation 4 :

Suppose, an individual has two accounts, in different scheduled banks, in the same town or different towns. He withdraws Rs.16,000 from the one account with a scheduled bank and Rs. 15,000 from another account with another scheduled bank. The aggregate withdrawals are Rs. 31,000.

As the withdrawals are from two different accounts with two different scheduled banks, they should not be regarded as taxable banking cash transactions, for the reasons discussed above.

Liability to tax and liability to pay

9.8 As noted above, the liability to tax is on a person effecting the withdrawal for receiving the money. However, the liability for collection and payment are shifted to scheduled banks.

Accordingly, a person liable to tax is not obliged to pay tax or comply with any formality in relation thereto. It may also be noted that there is no provision for payment or recovery of BCTT from a person liable to tax. In a case where the scheduled bank does not collect and/or pay BCTT, the tax authorities cannot recover the same from a person who is liable to tax. However, the tax authorities can recover the same from the scheduled bank along with interest and the other necessary consequences may follow. Apparently, in such a case, if the scheduled bank is able to identify the person liable to tax, it may be able to recover the same from the person liable to tax. The scheduled bank will have to bear the interest or penalty, if any, for delayed or no collection or non-payment of BCTT.

The scheduled banks will have to collect the tax; pay the same to the Government; file return in respect thereof; comply with the procedural requirements and so on.

Thus, when a person withdraws Rs. 30,000 from a scheduled bank, the bank will collect tax of Rs. 30 at the time of withdrawal and, if it is not paid separately, it would be deducted from the withdrawal and the bank will hand over Rs. 29,970 to the person.

Procedural compliances

9.9 As noted above, the scheduled banks will have to :

◆ identify the taxable banking transactions

◆ collect tax

◆ pay tax

◆ maintain records in respect thereof and

◆ file annual return in respect thereof.

Apart from the above :

◆ an assessment may be made in respect of the return filed

◆ in the assessment, the scheduled bank will have to produce the records and satisfy the tax authorities about the correctness of the return

◆ in case of shortfall or non-payment, it may be liable to interest, penalty, etc.

◆ in case of shortfall or non-payment, even penalty provisions may be attracted

◆ in case of any disagreement, the scheduled bank is entitled to file an appeal.

The Chapter makes provisions in respect of all the above requirements in all aspects relating to BCTT, as noted in the summary.

The provisions are more or less on the same lines as under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

account, generally or as per accounting theory and practice or terminology, as per Kohler's dictionary (Sixth edition, page 70) reads as follows:

"(i)

Any journal, register, or ledger which forms a part of a system of accounts.

(ii)

All the books of original entry and book of final entry, and the invoices, vouchers, contracts, correspondence, and the like that result from the occurrence of transaction and the operation of the system of accounts; often shortened to books". Thus, books of account could mean the day books, ledgers, memorandum records, supporting documents, vouchers, invoices, evidences and other records, which form part of system of accounts.

Under the Act, certain assessees are required to maintain books of account to enable computation of income or total income. In that, the exception is where the assessee is carrying on eligible business and opts for presumptive taxation.

It may so happen that an assessee may not comply with the requirement of maintaining books of account.

Prima facie, in case of a person who is not required to maintain the books of account, in terms of the applicable provisions of the Act, as well as a person who does not maintain any books of account, provisions of the section cannot apply; however, if any record or document is found, which can constitute books of account, the provisions of the section can be applied. To illustrate, in case of a person:

carrying on business and not maintaining books of account but compiling some information for calculating profit, possesses certain fake invoices which are taken into account for calculating the taxable income, it can be said that the use of fake invoices constitutes false entry in books of account and accordingly the section can apply;

not having business income and not maintaining books of account, if any document is found, which is not genuine and basis that, say, a claim for expenditure is made by the person, penalty under the section may not be attracted;

not having business income and maintaining books of account, if any document is found, which is not genuine and basis that, say, claim for expenditure is made by the person, penalty under the section may be attracted.

Having regard to the general meaning as well as the definition of books of account, it can be inferred that any document basis which a transaction is recorded in books of account or entry is made in books of account can form part of books of account.

It is held by courts that bank passbook or bank statement does not constitute books of account [CIT v. Bhaichand N. Gandhi (1982) 141 ITR 67 (Bom); Smt. Ramilaben B. Patel v. ITO (2018) 174 ITD 694 (Ahd. - Trib.)]

Under the Act, a person carrying on business is obliged to maintain books of account, as per section 44AA in the specified circumstances. A person not having business income, as such, in terms of the provisions of the Act is not obliged to maintain books of account. However, an assessee may voluntarily maintain books of account even in respect of income other than business income.

In case of a person carrying on the business maintaining books of account, obviously, the section can apply. In case of the person not carrying on business and maintaining books of account, basis the provisions of the section, it can be said that the section can apply. The section does not refer to the books of account as the one required to be maintained under the Act; it can include the books of account voluntarily maintained.

MERE ASSUMPTION OF SOME NON-EXISTENT FACTS - ISSUE OF SCN

In P. Ezhilpandian v. K. Vikash, DCIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 182 (PBPTA - AT), the facts of the case were that the appellant was an employee and was acting as librarian and sports coordinator of a college run by a Trust. In course of search of the Trust, it was found that the Chairman has given Rs. 15 lakhs in cash to the appellant to organize a football match. Accordingly, the same amount was handed over to Foot Ball Association. This amount was given during demonetization period. At the instance of the department the said amount was collected back and handed over to the department. The IO assumed that the said amount was given to the appellant in the guise of a loan in demonetized currency and to pay the same back subsequently in new currency. Accordingly, IO issued notice under section 24(1) despite the fact that the Trust confirmed that the amount was given to employee to handover same to Football Association for organizing a match. The IO disbelieved the same and issued provisional attachment notice under section 24(3) attaching the bank account of the employee. On basis of these facts, the Appellate Tribunal held as under:-

The appellant was only a facilitator to carry the cash to be handed over to the Football Association.

He was never the owner of the cash as a benamidar.

He had not deposited the cash in the bank which was provisionally attached by the IO without taking into account the facts of the case.

In fact, while attaching the bank account, no property existed which the appellant can alienate.

It was observed that there was no reason to believe by application of mind to the facts of the case while attaching the bank account. Notice was issued in a mechanical manner.

It was observed that every cash transaction cannot be termed as a benami transaction unless the transaction squarely falls under the stipulations of section 2(9)(A), satisfying the twin conditions: firstly, the property being held by a person who has not provided the consideration; secondly, the property is held by that person for the immediate or future benefit, direct or indirect of the person who has provided the said consideration.

The burden of proof of existence of a benami transaction lies on the authorities i.e. the person who alleges that transaction is benami as held in the case of Sitaram Agarwal v. Subrata Chandra [2008] 7 SCC 716.

The order of Adjudicating Authority confirming the order of the IO was set aside.

It would, thus, appear that the Amending Act was intended to cure an infirmity as revealed by the judgment of the High Court and to validate the past levy and collection of tax in respect of all kinds of non-lubricating mineral oils, including furnace oil, with effect from April, 1964. The fiscal enactments brought on the statute book in that connection are sometimes challenged by the taxpayer in Courts of Law. The Courts then scrutinise the legal provision to decide whether the levy of tax is legally valid or suffers from some infirmity. In case the Court comes to the conclusion that the levy of tax is not valid as the legal provision enacted for this purpose does not warrant the levy of tax imposed because of some defect in phraseology or other infirmity, the Legislature quite often passes an Amending and Validating Act. The object of such an enactment is to remove and rectify the defect in phraseology or lacuna of other nature and to validate the proceedings, including realisation of tax, which have taken place in pursuance of the earlier enactment which has been found by the Court to be vitiated by an infirmity. Such an Amending and Validating Act in the very nature of things has a retrospective operation. Its aim is to effectuate and carry out the object for which the earlier principal Act had been enacted. Such an Amending and Validating Act to make “small repairs” is a permissible mode of legislation and is frequently resorted to in fiscal enactments. The contentions of the appellants in Krishnamurthi’s case that during a part of the period for which retrospective operation to the said Amending Act had been given, sales tax had not been realised by the appellants from the purchasers and, therefore, the Amending Act should be struck down, was also rejected by the Supreme Court. It was held that the fact that a dealer was not in a position to pass on sales tax to others could not affect the competence of the Legislature to impose the sales tax retrospectively and it was a matter of legislative policy.

3.6-8g REMEDY FOR PREVENTING LOSS OF REVENUE SHOULD BE REASONABLE - In an attempt to prevent loss of revenue and plug the loophole in evasion of tax, the Government should provide remedy proportionate to evil. It should be reasonable, and not assume the character of a confiscatory measure. The law in this behalf is well stated in the celebrated case - State of Madras v. V.G. Row.1 The following observations of Patanjali Sastri, CJ., have acquired the status of a classic statement:

“...the Court should consider not only factor such as the duration and the extent of the restrictions, but also the circumstances under which and the manner in which their imposition has been authorised. It is important in this context to bear in mind that the test of reasonableness, wherever prescribed, should be applied to each individual statute impugned, and no abstract standard, or general pattern of reasonableness can be laid down as applicable to all cases. The nature of the right alleged to have been infringed, the underlying purpose of the restrictions imposed, the extent and urgency of the evil sought to be remedied thereby, the disproportion of the imposition, the prevailing conditions at the time, should all enter into judicial verdict. In evaluating such elusive factors and forming their own conception of what is reasonable, in all the circumstances of a given case, it is inevitable that the social philosophy and the scale of values of the Judges participating in the decision should play an important part, and the limit to their interference with legislative judgment in such cases can only be dictated by their sense of responsibility and self-restraint and the sobering reflection that the Constitution is meant not only for people of their way of thinking but for all, and that the majority of the elected representatives of the people have, in authorising the imposition of the restrictions, considered them to be reasonable.”

Even where an assessment has to be made ex parte, the information available should be reasonably weighed and a proper estimate made in the exercise of best judgment in the circumstances. There should be no tendency to frame assessments even in such cases mechanically on past basis, if there is evidence to the contrary, e.g., the business of the concern has become defunct or is in clearly adverse circumstances. If unjustified over-assessments are avoided, this will, inter alia, curtail the feature of exaggerated demands which unnecessarily inflate arrears figures.—Instruction : No. 574, dated 27-7-1973; Source : 193rd Report of Public Accounts Committee (1983-84) (Seventh Lok Sabha), (pp. 26-27).

Assessment of Banks - Checklist for deductions - In a recent review of assessment of Banks carried out by C&AG, it has been observed that while computing the income of banks under the head 'Profit and Gains of Business & Profession', deductions of large amounts under different sections are being allowed by the Assessing Officers without proper verification, leading to substantial loss of revenue. It is, therefore, necessary that assessments in the cases of banks are completed with due care and after proper verification. In particular, deductions under the provisions referred to below should be allowed only after a thorough examination of the claim on facts and on law as per the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 :

(i)

Under section 36(1)(vii) of the Act, deduction on account of bad debts which are written off as irrecoverable in the accounts of the assessee is admissible. However, this should be allowed only if the assessee had debited the amount of such debts to the provision for bad and doubtful debt account under section 36(1)(viia) of the Act, as required by section 36(2)(v) of the Act.

(ii)

While considering the claim for bad debts under section 36(1)(vii), the Assessing Officer should allow only such amount of bad debts written off as exceeds the credit balance available in the provision for bad and doubtful debt account created under section 36(1)(viia) of the Act. The credit balance for this purpose will be the opening credit balance i.e., the balance brought forward as on 1st April of the relevant accounting year.

(iii)

Section 36(1)(viia)(a) of the Act provides that in respect of any provisions for bad and doubtful debts of the type referred to in that sub-clause made by a bank, an amount not exceeding 5 per cent up to 31st March, 2003 and thereafter 7.5 per cent of the total income (computed before making any deduction under this clause and Chapter VIA of the Act) and an amount not exceeding 10 per cent of the aggregate average advances made by 'rural branches' of such banks computed in the manner prescribed under the Income-tax Rules, 1962, shall be allowed as deduction. For this purpose—

(a)

Total income of the year should be worked out after adjusting brought forward losses, if any, but before making any deductions under Chapter VIA of the Act.

(b)

The deduction for provision for bad and doubtful debts should be restricted to the amount of such provision actually created in the books of the assessee in the relevant year or the amount calculated as per provisions of section 36(1)(viia), whichever is less.

(c)

For working out the aggregate average advances by rural branches, the Assessing Officer should verify whether the branch(es) in question actually qualify to be categorized as 'rural branches' as per the definition in Explanation (ia) below section 36(1)(viia). The aggregate average advances of such rural branches should thereafter be computed in accordance with rule 6ABA of I.T. Rules, 1962.

(iv)

Third proviso to section 36(1)(viia) of the Act, allows a scheduled bank or non-scheduled bank, at its option, to claim a further deduction in excess of the limits specified in the preceding two provisos, for an amount up to the income derived from redemption of securities made in accordance with a scheme framed by Central Government. Before allowing deduction under this provision, it should be ensured that such income has been disclosed in the return of income under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession".

If income tax can be collected without any power of arrest, why powers of arrest are required under service tax?

(1)

(2)

Once the payment by non-account payee cheque/DD exceeds the limit of Rs. 2,00,000 specified in section 269ST, the particulars of such transactions will have to be reported under this clause irrespective of whether the receipt is on capital account and revenue account or whether the receipt is taxable or tax-exempt.

(3)

Where receipt is by cheque or demand draft, there will be practical difficul- ties in verifying whether the relevant receipt or payment is by account payee cheque or account payee draft. In such cases, the tax auditor should verify the transactions with reference to such evidence which may be available. In the absence of satisfactory evidence, the tax auditor, in his report may make comment in Clause (3) of Form No. 3CA that "It is not possible for me/us to verify whether the receipts/payments have been accepted/made otherwise than by an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft, as necessary evidence is not in the position of the assessee".

(4)

Tax auditors should take care to strike off or omit "me" or "us" inapplicable from the above comment.

(5)

The assessee may have purchased goods or services while simultaneously selling goods or services to the same party, with a consideration for exceeding Rs. 2 lakh. In such a case, if the amount of consideration for purchase is set off against the amount receivable for the sale of goods or services, such set-off is not a receipt as contemplated under section 269ST. Suppose the amount of such set-off exceeds Rs. 2 lakh. In that case, the tax auditor may give an appropriate note in Clause (3) of Form No. 3CA to the effect that such set-off not being a receipt or payment has not been included in the particulars given and the relevant sub-clause.

(6)

The words "each receipt in an amount exceeding the limit specified in section 269ST" in the opening line of clause 31(bc) suggest that consolidated reporting of consolidated figures mentioning 'various parties' will not suffice. However, where the receipts pertain to a single transaction or transactions relating to one event or occasion, such receipts may be grouped together while reporting.

(7)

The tax auditor may also keep in his record the date of the payments reported under clause 31(bc), although not required to be reported under the said clause.

17.5-5 Impracticable seizure of bank lockers and bank accounts [Section 247(4) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(3) of the ITA 1961)] While Section 132(1) of the ITA 1961 grants the power to seize money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable articles, Section 132(3) comes into play where it is not practicable to seize such assets. The Kerala High Court, in the case of ITO v. M. Shajahan [1976] 104 ITR 347 (Kerala), held that action under section 132(3) for a bank account is indeed permissible when it is not practicable to seize the asset. The Court observed that monies deposited in a bank, by virtue of the debtor-creditor relationship between the bank and the customer, are impracticable to seize in the physical sense. The money becomes the bank's property, and the customer merely has the right to demand repayment. Therefore, a prohibitory order under section 132(3) is the appropriate mechanism to prevent the assessee from dealing with such funds. The Court further clarified that while the proper procedure is to address the order to the customer (assessee) directing them not to deal with the money, with a copy communicated to the bank, an order directly issued to the bank would still have the same effect of preventing the assessee from operating the account. This is because section 132(3) also allows the officer to take "such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with this sub-section."

In contrast to bank accounts, the treatment of bank lockers under Section 132 is distinct. The Kerala High Court in M. Shajahan (supra), while discussing the nature of bank deposits, also touched upon bank lockers. The Court noted that with regard to securities and valuables deposited for safe custody in a locker, "the property in them remains with the customer." This implies that the contents of a bank locker are considered to be in the assessee's possession, even if physically held by the bank for safe custody. Therefore, if the contents of a locker are found to be undisclosed assets during a search, they can be directly seized under section 132(1)(iii). If, for some reason, direct seizure is not immediately practicable (e.g., due to lack of immediate access or valuation issues), then a prohibitory order under section 132(3) can be issued to prevent the assessee from operating the locker.

This distinction is crucial as for bank accounts, a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) is the primary mode of attachment due to the nature of the debtor-creditor relationship, making physical seizure impracticable. For bank lockers, direct seizure under Section 132(1) is possible; only if that is impracticable is a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) resorted to.

Under the ITA 1961, there was no explicit mention of bank lockers and bank accounts under Section 132. But, it was understood that the said items may fall within the ambit of the phrase "other valuable article or thing", if other conditions of section 132 are satisfied.

However, the ITA 2025 has explicitly included bank lockers and bank accounts under section 247(4), wherein the seizure of such items is not practicable.

17.5-6 Examination on oath of any other person present in the premises, etc. [Section 247(6) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(4) of the ITA 1961)]

Under the ITA 1961, the authorised officer could examine on oath only any person found to be in possession or control of any books of account, other documents, etc.

However, under the ITA 2025, the said authorised officer may also examine on oath any other person who—

(a)

Possesses or controls any information in electronic form or on a computer system

(b)

Has access to such a computer system

(c)

Is present in the premises; or

(d)

Is being searched.

In support of this amendment, the Ministry stated before the Select Committee that "During search, situations arise where a person though not possessing any books or other documents but is in the know of the business intricacies or is a key person managing business e.g. accountant, machine operator in the manufacturing industry, gatekeepers who are maintaining exit records, quality control persons who have complete production information and so on. Statements of such persons also become extremely important. Therefore, practically, these statements are relevant to conduct investigations. It is relevant to note that such statements are taken during the course of the search and at the premises being searched. Thus, the amendment has been rightly made to rationalise the provision."

As per rule 159(2) of CGST Rules, 2023 amended w.e.f. 26-10-2023, the Commissioner shall release attachment order by issuing order in form GST DRC-23.

There is no specific procedure prescribed for release of provisional attachment. Hence, GST Investigation wing of CBIC, vide circular No. GST/INV/Provisional Attachment/Advisory/2023-24, dated 2-9-2023, has advised that when period of provisional attachment has expires, the Commissioner shall issue communication/an intimation to the concerned authority/bank, drawing attention to the particulars of the Order/Form DRC-22 (which made the provisional attachment) and the provisions of section 83(2) of the CGST Act, 2017, and further indicating the release/restoration of the relevant property/account, in terms of those provisions. This intimation shall be copied to the person concerned.

Provisional attachment ceases when appeal filed with pre-deposit - Provisional attachment ceases when appeal is filed with mandatory pre-deposit - Benito Operations v. Dy Commissioner (2025) 112 GST 52 = 177 taxmann.com 636 (Del HC DB).

Powers of provisional attachment should be used carefully as powers are drastic - In Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2021] 6 SCC 771 = 86 GST 665 = 127 taxmann.com 26 (SC), it was observed that power to order a provisional attachment of property of taxable person including a bank account is draconian in nature. Exercise of power for ordering a provisional attachment must be preceded by formation of an opinion by Commissioner that it is necessary so to do for purpose of protecting interest of government revenue. Under provisions of rule 159(5), person whose property is attached is entitled to dual procedural safeguards - (a) An entitlement to submit objections on ground that property was or is not liable to attachment; and (b) An opportunity of being heard.

Powers of provisional attachment are drastic and should be exercised only if there is sufficient material on record that assessee is about to dispose of his property with a view to thwarting ultimate collection of demand. Provisional attachment should not be equated with attachment of property in the course of recovery proceedings - Valerius Industries v. UOI (2019) 109 taxmann.com 218 (Guj HC).

An order of provisional attachment cannot be as a matter of course. It is one of the drastic measures which the authority may be compelled to take if the situation demands for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government Revenue. When there are plethora of judgments explaining Section 83 in details, then why so much of litigation in the High Court. The only reason that can be attributed is the mechanical exercise of power under section 83 of the Act. This should stop at the earliest - Vinodkumar Murlidhar Chechani v. State of Gujarat [2021] 124 taxmann.com 272 = 45 GSTL 209 (Gujarat HC DB).

Powers under rule 86A are drastic and far reaching powers. The powers cannot be used as tool of harassment. Utilisation of credit is a vested right - S S Industries v. UOI (2021) 87 GSTR 71 = 57 GSTL 13 (Guh HC) - quoted and followed in PMW Metal v. UOI (2024) 91 GSTL 4 = 23 Centax 317 (Guj HC DB).

ACIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 276 = 241 Taxman 315 (Guj HC).

Really, if cash credit account is blocked, the account cannot be operated even if the person has limit available in cash credit account. Thus, he surely suffers.

Provisional attachment ceases after final order passed - Once final order is passed under section 74(9) of CGST Act, proceedings under provisional attachment order come to an end - Usha Industries v. Dy. Commissioner (2021) 88 GST 646= 128 taxmann.com 269 (P&H HC DB).

Procedure for provisional attachment and release of property - Order for provisional attachment shall be in form GST DRC-22. Objection to order of attachment shall be in form GST-DRC-23A. If payment is made by defaulter, or on expiry of a period of one year from the date of issuance of order under rule 159(1), whichever is earlier, the property can be released by issuing order in form GST DRC-23 - rule 159(2) of CGST Rules, 2017 [words in italics inserted w.e.f. 26-10-2023]

Departmental guidelines for provisional attachment - CBI&C, vide letter No. CBEC-20/16/05/2021-GST/359 dated 23-2-2021, has issued guidelines for provisional attachment. The guidelines are summarized below -

The powers of provisional attachment are extraordinary and should be resorted to with utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution.

Collective evidence should indicate prima facie case against tax payer before going ahead with provisional assessment.

If property attached is perishable/hazardous nature, it shall be released to taxable person after payment of market price of such property or amount payable by taxable person, whichever is lower.

Provisional attachment should not be resorted to in case of violations of technical nature. These should be resorted mainly in cases of evasion of tax or availment of wrongful Input Tax Credit. Like bogus invoices, frauds etc.

Normally, only immovable property should be attached. Movable property should be attached only if immovable property is insufficient to protect interests of revenue.

Property attached should not be excessive. More than one property can be attached and at different points of time.

Attachment should not hamper normal functioning of taxable person. Thus, raw materials and inputs for production or finished goods should not be normally attached.

Title deeds of immovable property should be checked

After provisional attachment, investigation and adjudication should be completed fast so that tax, interest and penalty can be recovered and purpose of provisional attachment is achieved.

Following property cannot be attached - (a) Property exempted from attachment by Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (b) Property for sale for execution of a decree of Civil Court.

42.10 Transfer of property to be void in certain cases

Where a person, after any tax has become due from him, creates a charge on or parts with the property belonging to him or in his possession by way of sale, mortgage, exchange, or any other mode of transfer whatsoever of any of his properties in favour of any other person with the intention of defrauding the Government revenue, such charge or transfer shall be void as against any claim in respect of any tax or any other sum payable by the said person - section 81 of CGST Act.

However, such charge or transfer shall not be void if it is made for adequate consideration in good faith and without notice of the pendency of such proceeding under this Act or, without notice of such tax or other sum payable by the said person, or with the previous permission of the proper officer - proviso to section 81 of CGST Act.

Officer empowered to exercise powers under proviso to section 81 - 'Proper Officer' to permit creation of charge, for the purpose of CGST is Additional Commissioner/Joint Commissioner of Central Tax, vide CBE&C circular No. 3/3/2017-GST dated 5-7-2017 [State Government will prescribe 'proper officer' for purpose of SGST in the respective State].

42.11 Tax to be first charge on property except under Insolvency Code

Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law for the time being in force, save as otherwise provided in the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, any amount payable by a taxable person or any other person on account of tax, interest or penalty which he is liable to pay to the Government shall be a first charge on the property of such taxable person or such person - section 82 of CGST Act.

Insolvency Code overrides section 238 of CGST and SGST Act - Insolvency Code overrides section 238 of CGST and SGST Act. Thus, property of following can be provisionally attached - (a) person who is availing bogus Input Tax Credit (b) Person to whom SCN has been issued under section 73 or 74, or recovery proceedings under section 79 have been commenced (c) Audit, search, seizure or arrest is under progress.

The assessee by stating that there was no banking facility does not seek to bring their case under clause (j) of rule 6DD but on account of the factual position. On 29-11-2002, the Punjab National Bank sends a letter to SLM directing them to close the bank account with State Bank of India and directs them to do all banking transactions only through the Punjab National Bank. This direction has come because the said Bank was appointed as the operating agency to implement a scheme of revival of SLM as framed by the BIFR. Therefore, SLM cannot flout the direction. The said company was carrying on business and it appears that the assessee was one of the major entities with whom they had entered into agreement. There was an agreement for 'conversion job-work' dated 1-4-2003. Even prior to that, on 27-2-2004, the Punjab National bank informs SLM that their bank account with them has been attached pursuant to an order passed by the Employees State Insurance Corporation, Madurai and the interest payable towards Punjab National Bank cannot be serviced from the very same account. On receipt of the letter on 2-4-2004, SLM writes to the assessee informing this development and requesting them to pay cash for meeting the wages, salary and other expenses for their unit to run smoothly. Further, they have represented for payment of additional conversion charges depending upon the quality of the product as they have incurred lot of expenses in modernising the machineries. These factors led to the assessee effecting payments in cash. The words 'extent of banking facilities available' in proviso to section 40A(3) has to be interpreted in the facts of a given case and all such cases will not be covered under clause (j) of rule 6DD which has been subsequently deleted. In the instant case, banking facility was available but the bank account of SLM could not be operated by the very bank themselves because of an order of attachment passed by the ESI department. SLM virtually came to the assessee with the begging bowl and requested to effect payment in cash. The assessee has entered into an agreement for conversion on job work basis. The assessee is required to act as a prudent businessman, so that the job-work is completed to his satisfaction with optimum quality. This has led the assessee to effect payments in cash The argument of the revenue is on the ground that in order to avoid the attachment of the bank account the assessee has effected payment in cash. It is to be noted that what is relevant to be seen insofar as section 40A(3) is concerned is the conduct of the assessee and not the payee and the question would be did the assessee have a reasonable cause to effect payment in cash. If the assessee has a reasonable Explanation, then the proviso under section 40A(3) would stand attracted and the assessee would be entitled to relief. It maybe true that merely because the payee is identifiable, it will automatically exonerate the assessee. The Court is not laying down any such broad principle. The fact that the payee was identifiable and not a fictitious person would go to show the bona fides of the transaction. This is what is required to be considered from the angle of a commercially expedient and prudent business house [Pr. CIT v. Sumukha Synthetics [2020] 119 taxmann.com 234 (Madras)]

(2) Is Section 40A(3) attracted where cash payments were made when bank accounts of the assessee were frozen by the Income Tax Department under Section 226(3)?

Where the Income Tax Department froze the bank account of the assessee under section 226(3) in those circumstances, the assessee would be entitled to exemption under rule 6DD in respect of cash payment and, therefore, no disallowance under section 40A(3) could be made.. Section 28BA of Customs Act make provision for provisional attachment of property of a person to whom show cause notice has been serviced under section 28 or 28AAA or 28B of Customs Act, if proper officer is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, to protect interests of revenue. 12.6-2d From the account(s) maintained by the recipient with the banker

(i) Generally, account and types

What is the meaning of "account"? It means a recipient's (ledger) account with the bank in/from which deposits/withdrawals are made and accounted.

The account(s) must be maintained by the recipient. Possibly, it implies that the recipient is the beneficial and the legal owner of the account(s), jointly or severally, and operates accordingly.

Any person can have a bank account in his own name; he may have more than one bank accounts; he may be having joint accounts with family members or others; he may be only a signatory in a bank account; the account of partnership or association of persons or a trust may be in the name of a person and so on.

In such a case, to ascertain the withdrawal in cash and that too beyond the threshold limit, which account or accounts need to be considered and can there be any aggregation?

(ii) Account held for Entities

Suppose, an individual is acting in the designated capacity for and on behalf of either a trust or any other entity, can it be said that the account is maintained by the recipient, that is, the individual? In such a case, it cannot be said that merely because an individual is a title holder or a signatory in a bank account for and on behalf of an entity, the account is maintained by him. In fact, the account maintained is of the trust or other entity.

(iii) Joint - Account

Suppose, an individual is a joint holder of a bank account along with his family members and others; such an account is also operated by the individual. The joint holding could be on account of various reasons and an individual may not necessarily have the beneficial ownership. Can such account be considered as maintained by all the joint holders jointly or severally? If it is joint, is it a separate account from the one maintained by the recipient? If it is considered as several, whether the transactions in such a joint account can be considered in the hands of all the joint holders? Mode and manner of dealing with such an account are not very clear from the provision and would pose several difficulties both to the banker as well as the recipients.

Would it be possible for a bank to take a view that in case of joint holding, the first name holder would be considered as the person withdrawing cash for the purposes of the section?

If there is joint ownership, another challenge would be in whose name TDS would be made and who would get credit for the same?

In the light of the above, the position may have to be determined having regard to the terms of contract, information relating to the same and clarifications which may be issued by the authorities from time to time in that behalf.

Depending on the treatment given by the banker in respect of the accounts held singly or jointly by any person, the person may have tax deduction from such bank account (whether belonging to him or otherwise) as well as additional information in respect of him furnished by the banker to tax department; if the person concerned has not reported, say, a bank account jointly held with another person and the other person has reported such bank account in his return, the first person will need to explain why the jointly held bank account was not reported and about debits and credits in such account.

Another issue which may have to be resolved is the manner of applying the threshold limit in case of joint banking account.

(iv) One or more accounts

A recipient has bank accounts in its own name with various branches of the bank; in such a case, it would be necessary to aggregate the transactions in all the bank accounts and accordingly discharge the obligations. The cash transactions in all the accounts, as they are with a single banking company, will have to be aggregated to enable the bank to discharge its obligations. Which branch should do it, may be the prerogative of the bank or can it be said that the bank branch from which the withdrawal is effected would be responsible for deducting tax?

A person may have different types of banking account, like, saving account, current account, fixed deposit account, recurring deposit account and so on. Suppose, all the accounts are in the name of single individual. Prima facie, to ascertain the applicability of the provisions, the transactions in all the accounts may have to be aggregated.

(v) Foreign branch

Suppose, a resident recipient has an account with a foreign branch of any Indian bank and effects withdrawal from (in foreign currency) such a bank account, the moot question is whether the bank is obliged to apply the provision to such account?
